value.a:
The Minuty Prestige Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024 is our still rosé by the glass, $17 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Minuty, mee-nu-TEE, is one of the classic names of Provence rosé. The Prestige is a Grenache-led wine, pressed pale and bottled young, so it keeps its freshness.

In the glass it is the pale color Provence is known for, and the color is part of the appeal. It tastes dry and refreshing: white peach, wild strawberry and citrus zest, with a light mineral finish.

Its freshness and red fruit are made for tomatoes and shrimp, which is why it is the first pick with the Creole Tomato Tostada, whose raw tomatoes need a wine as bright as they are, and with the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, where the acidity meets the tomato-based Creole sauce and the fruit cushions the tasso. It is the second choice with the Gulf Fish en Papillote for the tomato and olive, and a natural glass in the courtyard on a warm afternoon.

value.a:
The Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir 2023 is our light red Burgundy by the glass, $18 on the current menu at breakfast and lunch and at dinner; the Binwise list still prints $17.

It comes from a father and son family domaine, Domaine Robert et Damien Martin at Davayé in the Mâconnais, southern Burgundy, founded in 1982 by Robert and run by his son Damien, dah-mee-EN mar-TAN.

In the glass it is a translucent ruby. It tastes light and silky: red cherry, raspberry and a touch of earth, with light tannin and fresh acidity.

A light red like this goes where a big red would bully the food. It is the first pick with the Blackened Tofu, whose earthy mushrooms it loves, and the second choice on six plates: the Rohan duck and the duck confit waffle, the steak tartare cannoli, the gumbo, the Eggs Hussarde, where it meets the red wine in the marchand de vin, and the Pecan Gulf Fish if the bordelaise is red-wine based.

It is served slightly cool, around 55 to 58°F, so it stays fresh.

The Louis Jadot Beaune 1er Cru 2023 is the dinner tasting's red, a 4 oz pour with the Redfish Véronique on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Louis Jadot, loo-EE zhah-DOH, is the Burgundy house behind it, and Beaune, BOHN, is the wine capital of Burgundy. Premier Cru is Burgundy's second-highest vineyard tier, and the highest in Beaune, which has no Grand Cru. This is Pinot Noir from Premier Cru vineyards there.

In the glass it is bright ruby. It tastes of bright red fruit, with a silky texture and a savory edge.

It is a talking point for red with fish: light enough for the redfish, low in tannin, and its red fruit loves the hibiscus-pickled grapes. It is also the second choice the guide offers with the Chateaubriand, finesse over power, but only if it can be poured à la carte. It is opened 20 to 30 minutes ahead so the young wine shows its perfume.

value.a:
The Domaine de Durban Beaumes-de-Venise Rouge 2024 is our Southern Rhône red by the glass, $19 on the current menu at breakfast and lunch and at dinner; the Binwise list still prints $18.

Domaine de Durban, dur-BAHN, is famous for its sweet Muscat, but this is the estate's dry red: a Grenache and Syrah blend from the Beaumes-de-Venise cru, BOHM duh vuh-NEEZ, in the Southern Rhône.

In the glass it is deep ruby. It tastes ripe and generous: dark cherry, plum, dried herbs and pepper, with round, soft tannins.

That ripeness and pepper stand up to spice and braise. It is the first pick with the Eggs Owen, whose short rib is braised in red wine under a red wine sauce, and with the Creole Hanger Steak and its chili crisp, where soft tannins keep the heat from turning bitter. It is the second choice with the daytime Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak. The sommelier may also suggest it with the duck on the dinner tasting.

Grenache is generous in alcohol, so a few minutes in the ice bucket keeps it in check with spicy plates.

value.a:
Domaine de Châteaumar's Cuvée Vincent Côtes du Rhône is the breakfast tasting's red, a 4 oz pour with the Petite Filet Mignon on the Traditional Breakfast; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Châteaumar, shah-toh-MAR, grows it as all Syrah from fifty year old vines on two parcels beside Châteauneuf-du-Pape, nine kilometers from Orange, farmed organically without certification. That is unusual in the south, where Grenache usually leads.

In the glass it is deep purple-red. It tastes juicy and soft: black raspberry, black pepper and gentle tannins.

It is just right for red meat at breakfast: its soft tannins meet the lean filet gently, its pepper picks up the garlic spinach, and its freshness cleans up the crisp rösti. It is served slightly cool, 58 to 60°F, to stay fresh in the morning.

No vintage is printed on the tasting menu, so the bottle is checked before a year is quoted, and it is the Côtes du Rhône, not the estate's Châteauneuf of the same name.

value.a:
The Moulin d'Issan Bordeaux Supérieur is our Bordeaux by the glass, $16 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner. The current menu prints the 2021 and the Binwise list the 2023, so the vintage is read at lineup.

It comes from the team behind Château d'Issan, a classic estate in Margaux, and it is named for a ruined seventeenth century windmill: moulin, moo-LAN, is French for mill. It is Merlot-led with Cabernet Sauvignon, aged partly in new barrels.

In the glass it is deep ruby. It tastes of cassis, plum and cedar, medium-bodied with polished tannins.

That structure is what a steak with béarnaise wants: the tannin binds with the beef and the butter, and the acidity resets the palate. It is the first pick with the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak at breakfast and lunch, and the second choice with the Petite Filet Mignon and the dinner Creole Hanger Steak. It is the classic, gentler priced alternative to a $70 glass of Rubicon with the Chateaubriand, and it suits the Roost Burger at the bar.

If a table takes a bottle, it is opened or decanted 20 to 30 minutes ahead.

value.a:
Inglenook Rubicon 2010 is our grand red by the glass, $70 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Rubicon is Inglenook's flagship, a Cabernet Sauvignon based wine from Rutherford in the Napa Valley, and our glass is the 2010, sixteen years old: a Napa legend with real age on it.

In the glass it is deep garnet. Age has softened the tannins, so it tastes powerful but silky: blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and earth.

That depth is made for the Roasted Chateaubriand and its sauce Foyot, whose lean tenderloin a young, firm Cabernet would dry out, and it suits both hanger steaks. It is the step up with the Petite Filet Mignon on the breakfast tasting and with the daytime hanger.

An older wine can throw sediment, so the bottle is kept upright and poured slowly, leaving the last inch behind, and the label is always presented. At $70 a glass, two glasses come close to a bottle, which is when the sommelier is the better call. How the open bottle is preserved between pours is confirmed at lineup.

value.a:
The Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet Sauvignon 2021 is the dinner tasting's red, a 4 oz pour with the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Paul Hobbs is the Napa winemaker behind it, and Coombsville, KOOMZ-vil, is one of Napa's cooler corners, near the town of Napa, so its Cabernet keeps its freshness.

In the glass it is deep, dark red. It tastes of dark fruit and cocoa on a firm structure.

The guide's reasoning is that duck breast is red and fatty enough to carry Cabernet: the tannin binds with the fat and the wine tastes rounder, the dark fruit meets the glazed peaches, and the candied hazelnuts echo the cocoa. A young Napa Cabernet against cane syrup peaches is a real tension, which is why the Damien Martin Pinot Noir stands as the lighter alternative.

It is young, so it is opened or decanted 30 to 60 minutes ahead. The duck plate itself is disputed, so the garnish it meets is confirmed with the kitchen.

value.a:
The Dr. Hermann Erdener Prälat Riesling Auslese 2014 is our sweet wine, sold as a 375 ml half-bottle at $80, at breakfast and lunch and at dinner; it is the only sweet wine sold à la carte.

Dr. Hermann, HAIR-mahn, is the Mosel estate behind it. Auslese, OWS-lay-zuh, means selected harvest, a tier above late-harvest Spätlese, and the fruit comes from the steep Erdener Prälat vineyard, one of the Mosel's famous slopes. Twelve years of age add depth.

In the glass it is golden. It tastes of apricot, honey and pineapple, with electric acidity that keeps the sweetness lively.

Because it is sweeter than our desserts, it never tastes sour beside them, so it is the first pick on seven plates: Bananas Foster, the bread pudding, the Lemon Tart, the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, and the sweet breakfast starters, the trifle, the Framboise French Toast and the baked apple. The half-bottle pours about four dessert glasses of 2 to 3 oz, so it is a wine to share and carry from a sweet starter to dessert.

value.a:
Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva is the dinner tasting's dessert wine, a 4 oz pour with The Snickers on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Banyuls, bahn-YOOLS, is a sweet fortified red, a vin doux naturel, from the schist terraces around Banyuls-sur-Mer in Roussillon, French Catalonia. It must be at least half Grenache noir, and the fermentation is stopped with neutral grape spirit so the grape's own sugar stays in the wine. La Tour Vieille, lah TOOR vee-AY, ages its Reserva the oxidative way.

In the glass it is a deep, browning red. It tastes of dried fig, walnut, caramel, coffee and orange peel.

It is the classic wine for chocolate: its sweetness keeps chocolate from turning it bitter, and its cocoa and coffee notes echo the dessert. It is the first pick with The Snickers, the Cherries Jubilee and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, and the sommelier may lead with it on Bananas Foster and the bread pudding, once a manager confirms it is poured outside the tasting.

Prisoner of Love is the gin drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $16.00. Like every drink on the list, it carries the title of a song from 1946, the year Brennan's opened.

The menu prints gin, Earl Grey tea, clarified heavy cream and orange flower water. Clarifying is the old milk punch technique, where the milk is curdled and strained off clear; it leaves a silky texture without the weight of cream. Which gin, how our bar clarifies the cream, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a fragrant, silky drink. It tastes of the bergamot in the tea and a floral orange note over the gin.

It is the drink for a gin lover who wants something gentler than a martini, and a good talking point for anyone curious about cocktail history: milk punch is an old New Orleans habit, and our Brandy Milk Punch, the cold, creamy kind, opens the Traditional Breakfast.

value.a:
To Each His Own is the orchard drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $18.00, named like the others for a song of the year Brennan's opened.

The menu prints three parts. Daron Fine Calvados, dah-ROHN KAL-vuh-dohs, is apple brandy from northern France; Fine is the youngest grade of Calvados, fresh and fruity. Lillet Blanc, lee-LAY BLAHN, is a light French aperitif wine, floral and citrusy. The quince liqueur brings a fruit between an apple and a pear, very fragrant. Which quince liqueur, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

value.a:
Brennan's Champagne Cocktail is the house's bubbly classic at Bubbles at Brennan's, $20.00, our afternoon Champagne service in the Roost Bar and the courtyard, where it now sits beside four newer bubbly cocktails.

The menu prints three parts: Champagne, Angostura bitters, ang-guh-STOO-ruh, and a demerara sugar cube. That is the classic build, printed back in 1862: the cube is soaked in bitters, set in the glass, and the Champagne poured over it. Which Champagne, the glass and any garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a glass of Champagne with a steady stream of bubbles rising from the cube. It tastes dry and festive, with a soft spice from the bitters and a faint sweetness as the sugar dissolves.

It is the drink to offer anyone celebrating and a couple in the courtyard, and the grandest of the Bubbles cocktails. Champagne is sabered on Fridays at 5 pm, as the menu prints, and the hours are confirmed on shift.

Offer the Champagne Cocktail at Bubbles to anyone celebrating, to a couple in the courtyard, and on a Friday before the sabering. For a lighter round, the Riviera at $12.00 or the Chandon Garden Spritz at $15.00; in the Roost, the step up is the Flamingo at $28.00 or the Spoonbill at $36.00. Say: “Our Champagne Cocktail is the classic: Champagne over a sugar cube and Angostura bitters, festive and dry; on Fridays at five, stay for the sabering.”

Asked: What is in it?

Answer: Champagne poured over a demerara sugar cube with Angostura bitters, the classic build. Which Champagne we are pouring tonight, I will check with the bar.

Asked: When is the sabering?

Answer: Fridays at 5 pm, as the menu prints; I confirm it with the host stand each Friday.

Asked: When is Bubbles?

Answer: The menu prints Monday to Friday, 2 to 6 pm, in the Roost Bar and the courtyard; the hours are confirmed on shift.

Which Champagne is poured and the glass are not printed: confirm them with the bar before you name a house. The Bubbles hours are disputed between the menu and an older listing: confirm on shift, and check the courtyard is not privately booked. Do not confuse it with the Chandon Garden Spritz, which is sparkling wine, not Champagne. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Present the Champagne Cocktail the moment it leaves the bar, while the bubbles are still rising from the sugar cube: carry it by the stem or the base and set it down at the guest's right. Name it as it lands, and for a celebration toast the occasion in a word. If the bar finishes it at the table, stand back and let the guest watch the fizz climb from the cube. Say: “Here's our Champagne Cocktail: watch the bubbles rise from the sugar. Congratulations.”

Brennan's Bloody Mary is one of the classic eye openers, $11.00 at breakfast and lunch, the morning drinks New Orleans is known for.

The menu prints four parts: our housemade Bloody Mary mix, vodka, pickled okra and spicy beans. It is the eye opener for a guest who skips the beef in the Bloody Bull, our other Bloody classic, which is the same idea with beef bouillon stirred in for a richer, meatier drink. For a guest who wants a morning drink without alcohol, the Revive cold-pressed juice takes its place.

Offer the Bloody Mary to a guest who wants a savory eye opener but no beef, and to anyone who orders a Bloody Mary by name. For a guest who wants it richer, the Bloody Bull at $13.00; for a sweeter start, the Brandy Milk Punch at $12.00; without alcohol, the Revive cold-pressed juice at $10.00. value.a:
Revive Cold-Pressed Juice sits on the breakfast and lunch menu at $10.00, under Cold Pressed Juices, locally made and fresh squeezed, and is used in no pairing.

The menu prints its fruit: strawberry, apple and pineapple. Cold pressing squeezes the fruit without heat, which keeps the juice bright and lively. Who presses it for us, and whether another juice joins it, are questions for the bar.

The guest gets a glass of cold juice. It tastes fresh, sweet and fruity: strawberry first, with apple and the tang of pineapple.

It is the drink for a guest who wants neither alcohol nor caffeine, and for anyone who would like something light with breakfast. It suits a child or a guest who is not drinking and does not want coffee, and it gives a breakfast table a fresh option beside the eye openers.

Offer the juice to a guest who wants no alcohol and no caffeine, to a light breakfast eater, to a child, and to a guest who turns down the coffee. Next rounds: the Personality at $16.00 or Oh! What It Seemed to Be at $16.00 for something more like a cocktail. Say: “We also pour Revive, a cold-pressed juice of strawberry, apple and pineapple: fresh and bright, with no alcohol.”

Asked: What flavor is it?

Answer: Strawberry, apple and pineapple, as the menu prints it, pressed locally and served cold.

Asked: What does cold-pressed mean?

Answer: The fruit is squeezed without heat, which keeps the juice bright and lively.

Asked: Is there caffeine in it?

Answer: No, and no alcohol: it is simply cold-pressed fruit juice, a fresh start to breakfast and a good choice for a child at the table.

The menu prints one juice, Revive, with strawberry, apple and pineapple: name those, and ask the bar before promising any other. It is on the breakfast and lunch menu only, so a dinner guest asking for juice gets the bar's answer, not a promise. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

entries.value: Rare began as Piper-Heidsieck’s prestige cuvée and is now run as its own house, Rare Champagne; first vintage 1976, only about a dozen vintages ever declared. Chardonnay-led, from a single vintage: white peach, candied citrus, toasted almond and a long, fine mousse. Poured by the glass from an opened bottle kept fresh under the Coravin Sparkling stopper, which re-pressurizes it with CO2, so a single glass is possible. (The Binwise list and the Birthday Bubbles page print the 2012; the current Wines by the Glass page prints a 2013 Millésime at the same price: read the label.)

value.s10: The Durand, our Loire Sauvignon Blanc by the glass: crisp, herbal and bone-dry, one of the few wines that loves artichokes.
value.s20: Our Loire Sauvignon Blanc from the Durand family is bone-dry and zippy: grapefruit, cut grass and a flinty note. It's one of the few wines that really loves artichokes, so it's my pick with the Eggs Sardou.
value.s45: Our Sauvignon Blanc comes from the Durand family in France's Loire Valley, printed on the current menu as Famille Durand, Val de Loire. It's bone-dry and zippy: grapefruit, cut grass and a flinty note. Artichokes make most wines taste odd, but this one's sharp, herbal acidity stands up to them, which is why it's our first pick with the Eggs Sardou. It also loves tomatoes, fresh herbs and the crab claws. We keep it in the ice bucket so the acidity stays sharp.

value.a:
La Miraja Le Masche Barbera d'Asti 2023 is the newest red on our by-the-glass list, $16 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and our one Italian glass.

Barbera, bar-BEAR-ah, is the grape, and Asti the hill country of Piemonte in northwest Italy where it grows; La Miraja is the producer and Le Masche the name of the wine. How long it spends in barrel, and what Le Masche means, are questions for the sommelier.

In the glass it is deep ruby. Barbera is known for bright acidity and soft tannin, so it drinks juicy and medium-bodied: dark cherry and plum, fresh rather than heavy.

That acidity makes it a food red. It meets tomato, Creole sauce and cured pork, so it suits the shrimp and grits with their tasso and the Creole tomato tostada, and its soft tannin never fights a spicy plate. It is the first pick with Maggie's mushrooms, whose earthiness it lifts. On the list it sits between the light Damien Martin and the riper Durban.

Drappier Carte d'Or Brut is the first of our three Champagne half bottles on the Birthday Bubbles list, $75.00, poured for our 80th year at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Drappier, drah-pee-YAY, is a Champagne house, and Carte d'Or, kart DOR, is its Brut: a dry, non-vintage Champagne made by the traditional method. Our wine list carries Drappier among the grande marques, and lists the same Carte d'Or in a six liter Methuselah. The blend in the bottle is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a half bottle, 375 ml, presented and opened at the table, enough for two or three glasses. It tastes dry and crisp, with fine bubbles, citrus and orchard fruit and a toasty edge.

It is the gentlest priced way to toast with real Champagne when a full bottle is too much: a couple at breakfast, a birthday for two at dinner. Because the bottle is small, it is finished while it is still cold and lively.

value.a:
Paul Bara Grand Cru Reserve Rosé Brut is the rosé among our three Champagne half bottles on the Birthday Bubbles list, $120.00, poured for our 80th year at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Paul Bara, pol bah-RAH, is a grower producer in the Montagne de Reims: a family that grows its own grapes and makes its own Champagne, which is how our wine list files it. Grand Cru, grahn KROO, means the grapes come from the top rated vineyards. The blend and how the color is made are questions for the sommelier.

The guest sees a half bottle of pink Champagne, 375 ml, opened at the table, two or three glasses. It tastes dry, with red berry fruit, fine bubbles and a little more body than a white Champagne.

Krug Grande Cuvée Brut is the grandest of our three Champagne half bottles on the Birthday Bubbles list, $305.00, poured for our 80th year at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Krug, said kroog, is a Champagne house, and the Grande Cuvée, grahnd koo-VAY, is its prestige non-vintage Champagne. Krug numbers each Grande Cuvée by edition: our bottle list carries the 169th and the 170th. Which edition is in the half bottle is a question for the sommelier. Our menu prints it Grand Cuvée; the label and our wine list read Grande Cuvée.

The guest sees a 375 ml half bottle presented and opened at the table, two or three glasses. It tastes dry, deep and toasty, with fine bubbles and a long finish, and we serve it a touch warmer than the house bubbles so that depth shows.

It is the milestone toast for two: an anniversary, a big birthday, a guest who has always wanted to taste Krug. A half bottle makes that possible without the full bottle.

value.a:
Bollinger Special Cuvée Brut is the grandest of our magnums on the Birthday Bubbles list, $450.00, poured at breakfast and lunch and at dinner through our 80th year.

Bollinger, BOL-in-jer, is a Champagne house, and the Special Cuvée is its non-vintage Brut, known for a full, rich style. Our wine list carries it in the standard bottle too, beside the house's vintage La Grande Année. The blend is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a 1.5 liter magnum, two standard bottles in one, presented and opened at the table. It tastes dry and full, with toasty depth and firm acidity.

That richness carries a Champagne well past the first course, so it suits a table that wants one wine for the whole meal: the turtle soup, the gumbo, the Eggs Owen and even the Chateaubriand. It is the magnum for the guest who asks for Bollinger by name, and for a big table that loves a fuller Champagne.

Mirabelle Brut Rosé is the friendliest of the five rosé bottles on the Bubbles at Brennan's list: $50.00 during Bubbles, originally $80, in the Roost Bar and the courtyard on weekday afternoons from 2 to 6.

Mirabelle, meer-ah-BELL, is Schramsberg's sparkling label from California's North Coast, made by the traditional method, the same way as Champagne; our wine list carries Schramsberg too. It is a sparkling rosé, not Champagne, so we say sparkling rosé. The blend is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a bottle of pink sparkling wine opened at the table or the bar. It tastes dry, with red berry fruit and fresh bubbles.

It is the bottle for a group at Bubbles who want something pink to share without a big spend. Bubbles and salt are best friends, so it is the first pick with the fries and pink sauce, and lovely with the popcorn shrimp and the crawfish meat pies.

value.a:
Pommery Rosé Brut is the top of the five rosé bottles on the Bubbles at Brennan's list: $125.00 during Bubbles, originally $165, in the Roost Bar and the courtyard on weekday afternoons from 2 to 6.

Pommery, POM-er-ee, is a Champagne house in Reims, founded in 1836 and now part of Vranken-Pommery, the same group as the Charles Lafitte we pour on the tastings. Its rosé is a non-vintage Brut rosé Champagne. The blend is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a bottle of pink Champagne opened at the table or the bar. It tastes dry and crisp, with red berry fruit and fine bubbles.

It is the bottle for the big celebration at Bubbles, the group that wants the best pink Champagne on the list. It suits the cheese board and the crawfish meat pies, and a bowl of the Creole spiced nuts. The guide read the rosé range as Mirabelle to Pommery, and this is the top of it.

Asked: Is it the same as the Louis Pommery?

Answer: No: this is Champagne from the Pommery house in Reims, and the Louis Pommery is the California bottle on the same list.

Asked: How old is Pommery?

Answer: The house was founded in 1836, in Reims.

Asked: Is that the price all night?

Answer: The $125 is the Bubbles price, weekdays from 2 to 6; I will check with the manager what it is outside those hours.

value.a: Present the bottle and say Pommery Rosé, POM-er-ee, Champagne from Reims. Serve it at 43 to 46°F in a flute or tulip, from an ice bucket half ice and half water. Hold the cork and cage together, ease the cork out with a quiet sigh, and pour in two stages so the mousse does not overflow. Guests first and the host last. Say: “Pommery Rosé from Reims, our top pink Champagne. Cheers.”

value.s10: Fries with pink sauce, the easy bar basket to share over a glass of bubbles.
value.s20: Our fries come with pink sauce for dipping, crisp, salty and easy to share at $8. Salty fried food loves bubbles, so they're a natural with a glass of Champagne or a Chandon Garden Spritz.
value.s45: For something easy to share at Bubbles, the fries with pink sauce are $8: crisp, salty fries with our pink dipping sauce. Salt and fried food are the best friends a glass of bubbles has, because the acidity and the fizz clean the palate after every bite, so they're a natural with the house Champagne, a Chandon Garden Spritz, or a bottle of the Mirabelle rosé for the table. If you'd like to know what goes into the pink sauce, I'll ask the kitchen.

value.s10: Fried pickles: a medley of our housemade pickles, fried crisp, with chive cream.
value.s20: Our fried pickles are a medley of housemade pickles, crunchy outside and sour inside, with chive cream for dipping, $14. A crisp, bright drink is the match: the Albariño or a Riviera.
value.s45: Fried pickles are a Southern bar classic, and ours are $14 at Bubbles: a medley of pickles we make in house, fried so they're crunchy outside and sour and juicy inside, with a cool chive cream for dipping. That sourness wants a drink with as much acidity as the pickle, or the drink tastes flat, so I'd pour the Albariño, with its salty, citrusy snap, or a Riviera, Lillet Blanc with sparkling wine and lemon.

value.a:
Argyle Brut 2022 is the newest sparkling wine on our by-the-glass list and the friendliest priced, $15 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner. It is printed twice: on the Wines by the Glass page as Argyle Vintage Brut, and on the Birthday Bubbles page, under Champagne by the Glass, as Argyle Brut.

Argyle is the producer, in the Willamette Valley, wil-AM-it, in Oregon. So it is an American sparkling wine, not Champagne, whatever the page heading says, and we call it sparkling wine. Brut means dry, and 2022 is the vintage both lists print. The blend and how it is made are questions for the sommelier.

The guest gets a flute of dry bubbles; the sommelier gives the fuller tasting notes at lineup.

It is the glass for a guest who wants bubbles to toast the 80th without the house Champagne's price. Dry bubbles cut salt and fat, so it suits the Louisiana Oysters, and at Bubbles the popcorn shrimp and the fries with pink sauce.

value.a:
Cesarini Sforza Rosé Brut is the gentlest priced sparkling rosé on our bottle list, $55, filed under Selections Under $100, and a first pick for the popcorn shrimp at the Roost Bar.

Cesarini Sforza is a sparkling house in Trento, the city in the Trentino Alps of northern Italy that gives its name to the Trento DOC. Trento sparkling wine is made the way Champagne is: a still base wine is bottled with a little yeast and sugar, ferments a second time in the bottle and rests on its lees before release.

This rosé is mostly Chardonnay with a little Pinot Noir, which brings the pale pink color. In the glass it is dry and bright, with small red berries, a cool mountain acidity and a soft, easy mousse.

It is on the list for the guest who wants real bubbles at a friendly price. With the Crystal gastrique and fried shrimp, its cold fizz and red fruit cool the heat and scrub the batter.

value.a:
Asked: Is this Champagne?

Answer: No, Champagne only comes from Champagne in France. This is from Trento in northern Italy, made the same way, with the second fermentation in the bottle.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is Brut, so it is dry. The berry fruit can make it seem a little softer than it is.

Asked: What grapes are in it?

Answer: Mostly Chardonnay with a little Pinot Noir for the color; the sommelier can give the exact blend.

value.a:
Jansz Premier Cuvée Brut 2022 is the only Tasmanian sparkling wine on our list, $65, under International Sparkling, Australia, and a first pick for the Creole spiced nuts.

Jansz makes sparkling wine on Tasmania, the island south of mainland Australia. It is the coolest wine region in the country, and cool weather keeps the acidity high, which is what sparkling wine needs. Premier Cuvée is made by the traditional method, the Champagne method: a second fermentation in the bottle, then time on the lees before it is disgorged. The blend in this bottling is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is pale gold with fine bubbles. It tastes crisp and clean, citrus and green apple, with a touch of brioche from the lees and a salty snap at the finish.

Chapel Down Rosé Brut is the English sparkling rosé on our list, $75, filed under Selections Under $100, and the value bottle for the steak tartare cannoli.

Chapel Down is one of the best known sparkling wine producers in England, in the county of Kent in the southeast. Southern England is cool, with chalk soils much like those of Champagne, and the grapes keep the bright acidity sparkling wine needs. The rosé is made by the traditional method: a second fermentation in the bottle and time on the lees. The blend in this bottling is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is pale salmon pink with fine bubbles. It tastes dry and light, strawberry and red currant over a bright, almost tart acidity.

It is here for the guest who wants a pink sparkling wine that is a little unexpected. With the tartare, its red fruit sits beside the raw beef and its bubbles lift the crème fraîche and the crisp potato.

Ridgeview Bloomsbury Brut is one of four English sparkling wines on our list, three of them from Ridgeview, $75, under International Sparkling, England, and the value bottle for the Eggs Hussarde.

Ridgeview is a family sparkling wine estate at Ditchling in Sussex, on the chalk of the South Downs in southern England. Bloomsbury is its signature blend: mostly Chardonnay, with Pinot Noir and Meunier, the three grapes of Champagne. It is made by the traditional method, a second fermentation in the bottle and time on the lees before release.

In the glass it is pale gold with a fine, steady mousse. It tastes of green apple and lemon zest with a light toast of brioche, and the finish is crisp and clean.

It is on the list for brunch: a bottle of real traditional method bubbles that leaves room in the check for a second course. Its bright acidity cuts hollandaise and soft yolk, and the toast in it suits the Canadian bacon of the Hussarde.

value.a:
The Huet Pétillant 2019 is a lightly sparkling Vouvray, $90, filed under Selections Under $100, and a first pick for the fried pickles.

Domaine Huet is one of the great estates of Vouvray, on the Loire River near Tours, and it grows only Chenin Blanc, in three famous vineyards: Le Haut-Lieu, Le Mont and the Clos du Bourg. Our list carries all three as still wines. Pétillant means lightly sparkling: the wine is made by the traditional method, with a second fermentation in the bottle, but at a lower pressure than Champagne.

In the glass the bubbles are softer and creamier than Champagne’s. It tastes of quince, baked apple and honeysuckle, with the high, bright acidity Chenin keeps, and it is dry or very nearly so.

Ferrari Rosé Brut is the Trento sparkling rosé on our list, $95, under International Sparkling, Italy, and a first pick for the crawfish meat pies.

Ferrari is the best known sparkling house of Trento, in the Italian Alps, and it is no relation to the cars. It is run by the Lunelli family and makes only traditional method wines, with the second fermentation in the bottle, under the Trento DOC.

The rosé is Pinot Noir-led with Chardonnay. In the glass it is a soft salmon pink with a fine, creamy mousse. It tastes of wild strawberry and raspberry over fresh mountain acidity, dry, with a little more body than most pink sparkling wines.

It is on the list as the fullest sparkling rosé under $100. That body stands beside sweet crawfish, while the bubbles and acidity clear the fried pastry and the chive rémoulade, so each bite tastes as good as the first.

value.a:
JM Sélèque Solessence is a grower Champagne, $100, listed under Grower Producers, Vallée de la Marne, and a first pick for the fried pickles.

JM Sélèque is a family grower in Pierry, on the slopes just south of Épernay: they farm their own vines and make the wine themselves. Solessence blends Chardonnay and Meunier with a little Pinot Noir from seven villages, and part of it is fermented in oak barrels. It is Extra Brut, so very little sugar is added after the second fermentation.

In the glass it is pale gold with fine bubbles. It tastes of white flowers, ripe citrus and almond paste, with a chalky, precise finish, very dry and very clean.

It is on the list as a door into grower Champagne at a sweet spot price. Its dryness stands up to vinegar and its freshness lifts fried batter, which turns a snack at the Roost Bar into a bottle worth remembering.

value.a:
Billecart-Salmon Réserve Brut is a grande marque Champagne on our list, $115 the bottle, and a first pick for the crawfish meat pies.

Billecart-Salmon is a family house in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, in the Vallée de la Marne, founded in 1818 and still in the family. It is also the house that made our Brennan’s 80th Anniversary Sous Bois for the 80th year. The Réserve is its non-vintage Brut, blended from Meunier, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with reserve wines from earlier years for depth.

In the glass it is pale gold with very fine bubbles. The house style is fresh and delicate rather than heavy: pear, citrus and a light brioche, then a clean, bright finish.

It is on the list as the Champagne a server can recommend to anyone. The same wine comes in a magnum, a Methuselah and a 15 liter Nebuchadnezzar for a party. With the meat pies, its freshness cuts the fried pastry and the creamy rémoulade.

value.a:
Pierre Paillard Les Parcelles XVIII is a Grand Cru grower Champagne, $120, under Grower Producers, Vallée de la Marne on our list, and the sweet spot bottle for the Louisiana oysters.

Pierre Paillard is a family grower in Bouzy, a Grand Cru village on the Montagne de Reims famous for its Pinot Noir. Les Parcelles blends Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from the family’s own parcels in Bouzy, and the Roman numeral on the label identifies the blend; what it marks is a question for the sommelier. It is Extra Brut, with very little sugar added.

In the glass it is gold with fine, firm bubbles. It tastes of red apple, citrus peel and chalk, very dry, with the weight Pinot Noir brings.

It is on the list as a Grand Cru at a sweet spot price. With the barbecue oysters, its body meets the buttery sauce, its dryness and chalk love the brine, and the bubbles clear the fried saltine crumble.

value.a:
Louis Roederer Collection 244 is the house Brut of Roederer, $120 on our list among the grandes marques, and a first pick for the popcorn shrimp.

Louis Roederer is a family Champagne house in Reims, best known for Cristal, which is also on our list. Its non-vintage Brut is called Collection, and each blend carries a number. Collection 244 is built on the 2019 harvest and blended with wines from the house’s perpetual reserve, a store of older wine it tops up every year, with a small part of oak-aged reserve. The grapes are Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

In the glass it is pale gold with fine bubbles. It tastes fresh and precise: citrus, white peach and a light pastry note, crisp and long.

It is on the list as a great house’s Brut at a sweet spot price, and a quiet introduction to Cristal. With the popcorn shrimp, its bubbles cut the batter and its freshness cools the Crystal gastrique.

Chartogne-Taillet Rosé Brut is a grower rosé Champagne, $125, under Grower Producers, Montagne de Reims on our list, and the sweet spot bottle for the steak tartare cannoli.

Chartogne-Taillet is a family grower in Merfy, a village northwest of Reims, and the family makes the wine from its own vines. The rosé is colored by blending in a little red wine made from Pinot Noir grown in Merfy. The rest of the blend is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is a pale copper pink with fine bubbles. It tastes of red currant and wild strawberry, dry, with a savory, chalky finish rather than sweet fruit.

It is on the list for the guest who wants pink Champagne with character. With the tartare, the red fruit sits beside the raw beef, and the freshness lifts the egg yolk and bottarga.

value.a:
Larmandier-Bernier Longitude is an all-Chardonnay grower Champagne, $135, under Grower Producers, Côtes de Blancs on our list, and the sweet spot bottle for the Grand Isle Jewel oysters.

Larmandier-Bernier is a family grower in Vertus, at the southern end of the Côte des Blancs, the chalk slope where Champagne’s finest Chardonnay grows. Longitude is a Blanc de Blancs, all Chardonnay, rated Premier Cru and named for villages that lie along the same line of longitude. It is Extra Brut, with very little sugar added.

In the glass it is pale, almost silver, with fine bubbles. It tastes of lemon, green apple and chalk, bone dry, with a salty, lingering finish.

It is on the list as the oyster Champagne of the sweet spot. Its chalk and acidity mirror the brine and the mignonette, and its bubbles calm the Fresno chili.

value.a:
Brennan’s Essential by Piper-Heidsieck is our house Champagne, and the full bottle is $140 on the list among the grandes marques. It is the sweet spot bottle for the Eggs Hussarde.

Piper-Heidsieck, a Champagne house in Reims, makes it for us, and the label carries the Brennan’s name. It blends Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay and is Extra Brut: very little sugar is added after the second fermentation.

The guest knows it from the glass; the bottle is the same wine opened at the table for the whole party. In the glass it is pale gold with lively bubbles. It tastes bone dry, with citrus, orchard fruit and brioche, and a firm, chalky finish.

Ordering the bottle makes sense for a table of four or more drinking Champagne through brunch. With the Hussarde, its acidity keeps the hollandaise light and its toastiness suits the coffee-cured Canadian bacon.

value.a:
Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label is the famous orange-labeled Champagne, $155 on our list among the grandes marques, and the name many guests ask for first.

Veuve Clicquot is a great house in Reims. Veuve means widow: Barbe-Nicole Clicquot took over the house after her husband died and ran it in the early nineteenth century, and she is remembered for the riddling table, the rack that gathers the yeast in the neck of the bottle so it can be removed. Yellow Label is the house Brut, Pinot Noir-led with Meunier and Chardonnay.

The label is called yellow but looks orange, and guests know it on sight. In the glass it is gold with lively bubbles. It tastes generous and toasty: ripe apple, citrus, brioche, round and dry.

It is on the list because guests ask for it by name, and a server should be able to say yes. It suits a toast, brunch, the turtle soup or the meat pies.

value.a:
Moët & Chandon Nectar Imperial Rosé is a sweet rosé Champagne, $180 on our list, and the sweet spot bottle for the Framboise French toast.

Moët & Chandon is the largest of the great Champagne houses, based in Épernay. Nectar Imperial Rosé is its demi-sec rosé: after the second fermentation it is finished with noticeably more sugar than a Brut, so it tastes gently sweet. It is Pinot Noir-led, with Meunier and Chardonnay.

In the glass it is a deep salmon pink with a creamy mousse. It tastes of ripe strawberry and raspberry with a soft, creamy sweetness, and the bubbles keep it from feeling heavy.

It is on the list for sweet plates. A sweet dish makes a dry wine taste sharp and thin, so a sweeter wine is the match. With the French toast, its berries echo the raspberry coulis and its bubbles lift the mascarpone mousse.

value.a:
Charles Heidsieck Réserve Brut is one of the richest non-vintage Champagnes on our list, $210 among the grandes marques, and a first pick for the Creole spiced nuts.

Charles Heidsieck is a Champagne house in Reims, and its wines age in the chalk cellars dug beneath the city. The Réserve is known for a high share of reserve wines, older wines held back from earlier harvests, blended into the Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier of the new year, and for long aging on its lees.

In the glass it is a deeper gold than most, with fine bubbles. It tastes rich and toasty: roasted nuts, brioche and dried apricot, creamy in texture, dry, with a long finish.

It is on the list for the guest who loves a fuller Champagne. Its nutty, toasted flavors echo roasted nuts and soften Creole spice, and it is lovely with the sherry in the turtle soup.

value.a:
Bollinger Special Cuvée is the classic full-bodied Champagne on our list, $250 the 750 ml bottle, and the sweet spot bottle for the turtle soup.

Bollinger is a family-owned Champagne house in Aÿ, a Grand Cru village famous for Pinot Noir. Special Cuvée is its non-vintage Brut: Pinot Noir-led with Chardonnay and a little Meunier. Part of the wine is fermented in oak barrels, and the house keeps its older reserve wines in magnums, which is unusual and adds depth.

In the glass it is a deep gold with fine, firm bubbles. It tastes rich and structured: baked apple, toasted nuts and a little spice, with a firm, dry finish.

It is on the list as the anchor of the rich style. With the turtle soup, its nutty depth echoes the aged sherry and lifts the brown butter spinach. For a party, the Birthday Bubbles list pours the same wine in magnum.

Armand de Brignac Brut Gold is the Champagne known as Ace of Spades, $325 on our list among the grandes marques. Guests ask for it by sight.

It is made by the Cattier family in Chigny-les-Roses, on the Montagne de Reims, and today it is owned in partnership by Shawn Carter, the artist known as Jay-Z, and Moët Hennessy. The Brut Gold blends Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier.

The bottle is the story: opaque, metallic gold, with a pewter ace of spades on the front. In the glass the wine is gold, with a soft, creamy mousse. It tastes ripe and generous, white peach, brioche and a touch of honey, dry but round.

It is on the list for the celebration that wants to be seen. Present it so the table can see the bottle, open it with care, and keep it iced: the metal-finished bottle takes longer to chill. It suits the oysters, the turtle soup and the BBQ lobster.

value.a:
Pol Roger Blanc de Blancs 2015 is a vintage, all-Chardonnay Champagne, $335 on our list, and the celebration bottle for the Poussin à la Moutarde.

Pol Roger is a family Champagne house in Épernay. Winston Churchill was its most famous admirer, and the house named its prestige cuvée Sir Winston Churchill after his death. This Blanc de Blancs is made only from Chardonnay grown in the Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs, and only from the 2015 harvest, so it is a vintage wine.

In the glass it is pale gold with a very fine, creamy mousse. It tastes of lemon, white flowers and chalk, with a long, precise finish and the first notes of toast that come with age.

It is on the list as a vintage Champagne for dinner, not only for a toast. With the fried Cornish hen, its chalky freshness cuts the crust and the mustard cream sauce and keeps each bite light.

value.a:
Bollinger PN TX20 is an all Pinot Noir Champagne, $345 on our list among the grandes marques, and the celebration bottle for the Louisiana oysters.

Bollinger is the family house in Aÿ, a Grand Cru village famous for Pinot Noir. Its PN series is a Blanc de Noirs, white Champagne made only from Pinot Noir, a black grape, and each edition is led by one village. TX20 is led by Tauxières, on the southwest slopes of the Montagne de Reims, and built on the 2020 harvest, with older reserve wines making up the rest.

In the glass it is gold with fine, firm bubbles. It tastes full and powerful: red apple and white peach, a chalky tension and a long, firm finish.

It is on the list as the Champagne for big flavors. With the barbecue oysters, its weight matches the buttery, peppery sauce while its bubbles clear the fried saltine crumble.

value.a:
Billecart-Salmon Cuvée Elisabeth Salmon Rosé 2009 is the house’s prestige vintage rosé, $450 on our list, and the celebration bottle for the steak tartare cannoli.

Billecart-Salmon is a family Champagne house in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, founded in 1818, and the house that made our Brennan’s 80th Anniversary Sous Bois. The house took its name from the marriage of Nicolas François Billecart and Elisabeth Salmon, and its grandest rosé carries her name. It is Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from the 2009 harvest alone, aged for years before release.

In the glass it is a pale salmon copper with a fine, silky mousse. It tastes of wild strawberry, blood orange and rose petal, with the savory, toasty depth that age brings, dry and long.

It is on the list for the grand celebration that wants pink. With the tartare, its depth meets the raw beef and its savory edge loves the bottarga and egg yolk.

value.a:
Bollinger La Grande Année 2015 is the vintage Champagne of Bollinger, $495 on our list, and a first pick for the crawfish meat pies.

Bollinger is the family house in Aÿ, a Grand Cru village famous for Pinot Noir. La Grande Année means the great year: it is made only from a harvest the house judges worthy, and this bottle is all 2015. It is Pinot Noir-led with Chardonnay, and every part of it is fermented in oak barrels, which is rare for Champagne and builds depth.

In the glass it is a deep gold with fine bubbles. It tastes rich and layered, baked apple, hazelnut, honey and spice, held together by firm acidity, with a long finish.

It is on the list as the vintage step up from the Special Cuvée. With the crawfish meat pies, its depth stands beside the sweet crawfish while its acidity cuts the pastry and the chive rémoulade.

value.a:
Jacques Selosse Initial is the cult grower Champagne on our list, $560, under Grower Producers, Côtes de Blancs, and a first pick for the fried pickles.

Jacques Selosse is a grower house in Avize, a Grand Cru village of the Côte des Blancs. Anselme Selosse, who took over from his father, made Champagne the way a great Burgundy domaine makes white wine, fermenting and aging in oak barrels, and inspired a generation of growers. Initial is a Blanc de Blancs, all Chardonnay, blended from several harvests, and the list prints its disgorgement date, 10.16.23, the day its yeast was removed.

In the glass it is a deep gold with fine bubbles. It tastes intense and vinous: ripe citrus, hazelnut, honey and a salty, mineral grip, with vivid acidity.

It is here because collectors ask for it and it is hard to find. Its acidity and salt meet the pickles head on and turn a snack into an occasion.

value.a:
Krug Grande Cuvée 170th Edition is Krug’s signature Champagne by the full bottle, $615 on our list, and a first pick for the Creole spiced nuts.

Krug is a Champagne house in Reims, founded in 1843, that makes only prestige Champagne. Grande Cuvée is blended from wines of many years and many plots, often well over a hundred wines, each first fermented in small oak casks. Every blend carries an edition number on the label, and ours is the 170th; the year it is built on is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is gold with very fine bubbles. It tastes deep and layered: toasted nuts, brioche, citrus peel and honey, with a very long finish.

It is on the list as one of the famous names a celebration asks for. Its toasted, nutty depth meets the spiced nuts, and it is grand with the turtle soup and the Chateaubriand.

Rare Brut 2013 is the full bottle of the prestige vintage we pour by Coravin, $650 on our list among the grandes marques, and the celebration bottle for the Eggs Hussarde.

Rare began as the prestige cuvée of Piper-Heidsieck, the Reims house that makes our Brennan’s Essential, and today it carries its own name. The 2013 is a single vintage, Chardonnay-led with Pinot Noir, aged for years on its lees before release.

In the glass it is gold with a long, fine mousse. It tastes of white peach, candied citrus and toasted almond, rich and elegant, with a long finish.

By the glass, Rare is poured through the Coravin, so a guest can try one glass without opening a bottle. The full bottle is for the table that wants the whole experience. With the Hussarde, its depth meets the coffee-cured bacon and the marchand de vin, while its freshness keeps the hollandaise light.

value.a:
Louis Roederer Cristal 2015 is one of the most famous Champagnes in the world, $775 on our list, and a first pick for the popcorn shrimp.

Roederer is a family house in Reims. Cristal was first made in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II of Russia, who asked for a clear bottle, and it has come in clear glass ever since. It is the house’s prestige vintage, made only in good years from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, here the 2015 harvest. Because clear glass lets light in, each bottle travels wrapped.

In the glass it is pale gold with silky, very fine bubbles. It tastes precise and pure: citrus, white peach, chalk and a light toast, with a long finish.

It is on the list because guests ask for it by name. Its precision cuts fried batter and makes the popcorn shrimp an occasion, and it is grand with the oysters and the crab claws.

value.a:
Krug Rosé is the most powerful pink Champagne on our list, $865 among the grandes marques, and the celebration bottle for the New Orleans shrimp and grits.

Krug is the Reims house that makes only prestige Champagne. Its rosé is built the way the Grande Cuvée is: wines from several years, each first fermented in small oak casks, then colored with a little red wine made from Pinot Noir. The blend includes Chardonnay and Meunier too.

In the glass it is a pale salmon copper with fine bubbles. It tastes powerful and spicy rather than sweet or pretty: red berries, blood orange, rose hip and toasted brioche, dry, with a very long finish.

It is on the list for the guest who wants the grandest rosé. Its red fruit and power stand up to Louisiana shrimp, smoky tasso and the fried pimento cheese grit cake, and it is glorious with the duck.

value.a:
Dom Pérignon P2 2006 is the long-aged release of the most famous prestige Champagne, $1260 on our list among the grandes marques.

Dom Pérignon is the prestige Champagne of Moët & Chandon in Épernay, named for the Benedictine monk at the abbey of Hautvillers who helped shape the making of Champagne. It is always a vintage, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. The house releases each vintage at more than one plénitude, a peak in its life: P2, the second plénitude, is the same wine kept on its lees for many more years before it is disgorged.

In the glass it is a deep gold with creamy bubbles. The 2006 tastes deep and smoky: toasted brioche, candied citrus, hazelnut and a little smoke, with a very long finish.

It is on the list for the guest who knows Dom Pérignon and wants its rarest form. It is grand with the oysters, the turtle soup and the lobster.

entries.target: wine:Salon ‘Le Mesnil’ Blanc de Blancs Brut 2013

value.a:
Salon Le Mesnil 2013 is one of the rarest Champagnes in the world, $2080 on our list among the grandes marques, and a name collectors ask for.

Salon makes one wine only: a Blanc de Blancs from Chardonnay grown in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, a Grand Cru village of the Côte des Blancs, from a single year. It is made only in the years the house judges exceptional, a handful in a decade; in other years the grapes go to its sister house, Delamotte. The 2013 was aged for about a decade before release.

In the glass it is pale gold with very fine bubbles. It tastes taut and chalky: lemon peel, white flowers and hazelnut, with a stony, very long finish that keeps unfolding.

It is on the list for the guest who knows exactly what it is. It opens slowly, so serve it in a wine glass and let it breathe. It is grand with the raw oysters and the crab claws.

Louis Jadot Beaujolais-Villages 2021 is the gentlest priced half-bottle on our list, $25 for 375 ml, filed under Burgundy red, Beaujolais, and the half-bottle for the New Orleans shrimp and grits.

Louis Jadot is a great Burgundy house based in Beaune, and our by-the-glass list pours its Beaune Premier Cru. Beaujolais-Villages is the appellation for the villages in the granite hills of northern Beaujolais, at the southern end of Burgundy. The grape is Gamay.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is a bright ruby. It tastes light and juicy, red cherry and raspberry with a little pepper, soft tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list as the easy red for brunch. Spice makes tannin taste harsh, so a soft, fruity red with a slight chill keeps the Creole sauce and the tasso in balance.

value.a:
Duckhorn Sauvignon Blanc 2023 is a crisp California white in a half-bottle, $35 for 375 ml, filed under United States Sauvignon Blanc as Duckhorn North Coast, and the half-bottle for the Creole Caesar.

Duckhorn Vineyards is a Napa Valley winery best known for its Merlot, which is also on our list in a half-bottle. Its Sauvignon Blanc is drawn from vineyards across California’s North Coast and made to stay fresh and bright.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is pale straw. It tastes crisp and clean: grapefruit, citrus and melon with a hint of fresh herbs and a little roundness.

It is on the list as a light lunch white. A dressing needs a wine with plenty of acidity, so it meets the smoked oyster dressing and the Grana Padano of the Caesar, and it is lovely with the crab and corn omelette.

It is on the list as a lighter white Burgundy for a starter. Its roundness meets the warm brown butter and its acidity matches the vinaigrette, while the fines herbes keep it fresh.

value.a:
Tribaut-Schloesser Origine is a grower Brut in a half-bottle, $50 for 375 ml, filed under Grower Producers, Vallée de la Marne, and a half-bottle to suggest with the Creole spiced nuts.

Tribaut-Schloesser is a family Champagne house in Romery, in the hills north of Épernay, founded in 1929. Origine is its Brut, Meunier-led with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from several villages, and a part of the reserve wine in it is aged in oak.

The guest sees a half-bottle, opened at the table, two or three glasses. In the glass it is pale gold with lively bubbles. It tastes fresh and fruity: pear and plum, a touch of brioche, and an easy, balanced finish.

It is on the list as a friendly Champagne for two at the Roost Bar. Salt makes wine taste fruitier and bubbles refresh after every handful, so it suits the spiced nuts, the fried pickles and the cheese board.

Domaine Huet is one of the great estates of Vouvray, on the Loire near Tours, and Le Haut-Lieu is the vineyard where the estate began. Sec means dry. It is all Chenin Blanc, and the 2019 has had a few years in bottle.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is a deeper gold than a young white. It tastes of quince, pear, beeswax and chamomile, dry and textured, with the bright acidity Chenin keeps as it ages.

value.a:
Huet Le Mont Demi-Sec 2023 is a gently sweet Vouvray in a half-bottle, $60 for 375 ml, filed under Loire white, Vouvray and Touraine, and the half-bottle for the baked apple and the duck confit waffle.

Domaine Huet is one of the great estates of Vouvray, on the Loire near Tours, and Le Mont is one of its three vineyards, with Le Haut-Lieu and the Clos du Bourg. It grows only Chenin Blanc. Demi-sec means half dry: the wine keeps some natural sweetness, balanced by Chenin’s high acidity.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of apple, pear, honey and white flowers, gently sweet and fresh, never heavy.

It is on the list for the sweet side of breakfast. A sweet dish makes a dry wine taste sour, so a wine about as sweet as the plate is the match: with the baked apple, its fruit and honey echo the apple and the glaze.

value.a:
Asked: What does Clos mean?

Answer: A vineyard enclosed by a wall. The Clos de la Mousse is a small walled Premier Cru in Beaune that Bouchard owns entirely.

Asked: Is it a light red?

Answer: Light to medium, silky, with fresh acidity; it will not overwhelm brunch.

Asked: How does it compare with the Beaune by the glass?

Answer: Both are Beaune Premier Cru; this one comes from a single walled vineyard, in a half-bottle.

entries.target: wine:Ridge Vineyards ‘Estate’ Cabernet Sauvignon Santa Cruz Mountains 2020 (375 ml)

value.a:
Ridge Estate Cabernet Sauvignon 2020 is a mountain Cabernet in a half-bottle, $110 for 375 ml, filed under United States Cabernet Sauvignon, Central Coast, and the half-bottle for the Roasted Chateaubriand.

Ridge Vineyards is famous for Monte Bello, the Cabernet from its vineyards high on a ridge in the Santa Cruz Mountains south of San Francisco. The Estate Cabernet comes from the same mountain vineyards. Whether it carries some Merlot or other grapes in this vintage is a question for the sommelier; Ridge prints its ingredients on the back label.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is deep purple. It tastes of blackcurrant, cedar and graphite with a savory herb note, firm tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list for beef. Protein and fat soften tannin, so it tastes rounder with the Chateaubriand and the sauce Foyot.

value.a:
Louis Jadot Meursault 2022 is a village white Burgundy in a half-bottle, $115 for 375 ml, filed under Burgundy white, Meursault, and the half-bottle for the Louisiana BBQ lobster.

Louis Jadot is a great Burgundy house in Beaune, and Meursault is the village of the Côte de Beaune best known for rich, nutty white Burgundy. This is Jadot’s village wine, all Chardonnay, aged in barrel; for how long is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is gold. It tastes of ripe lemon, hazelnut and toast, with a buttery roundness and fresh acidity.

It is on the list for the lobster course. A rich wine meets a rich plate: its roundness matches the lobster and its butter, and its acidity freshens the white bean stew and the ’nduja. The dinner tasting pours its own white with this course.

value.a:
La Cigarrera Manzanilla is a bone dry sherry in a half-bottle, $120 for 375 ml, filed under Fortified Wines, Spain, and the half-bottle for the turtle soup.

Manzanilla is the sherry of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the seaside town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir river in southern Spain, and La Cigarrera is a family bodega there. It is made from the Palomino grape and aged under flor, a living layer of yeast on top of the wine that keeps it pale and fresh and gives it a salty, bready tang. It is fortified, but light.

The guest sees a half-bottle and small pours. In the glass it is pale straw. It tastes bone dry: green apple, chamomile, almond and bread dough, with a salty sea breeze.

It is on the list for the soup. Our turtle soup is finished with aged sherry, so a dry sherry beside it repeats that flavor and cuts the richness.

Dow’s 2000 Vintage Port is a fortified dessert wine in a half-bottle, $120 for 375 ml, filed under Fortified Wines, Portugal, and the half-bottle for The Snickers.

Dow’s is one of the great Port houses of the Douro valley in northern Portugal, run by the Symington family, and its style is known for being on the drier side of Port. Vintage Port is made only in the best years, which the houses declare, and 2000 was a declared year. It is aged briefly in cask and then in bottle, where it throws a sediment. The grapes are a blend of Douro varieties; which ones is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a half-bottle and small pours. In the glass it is deep garnet. It tastes of blackberry, plum, dark chocolate and licorice, sweet and fortified, its tannin softened by age.

It is on the list for chocolate. A dessert wine should be at least as sweet as the dessert, so it carries The Snickers.

value.a:
Niepoort Colheita 1997 is a single harvest tawny Port in a half-bottle, $120 for 375 ml, filed under Fortified Wines, Portugal, and the half-bottle for the Café Brûlot coffee cake.

Niepoort is a family Port house of Dutch origin, based in Porto and the Douro valley in northern Portugal and known for aged tawnies. Colheita means harvest: a tawny Port from a single year, here 1997, aged for many years in old casks, where it slowly turns amber and nutty. The label carries the bottling date as well as the harvest.

The guest sees a half-bottle and small pours. In the glass it is amber. It tastes of walnut, caramel, dried orange peel, coffee and spice, sweet and silky, with a long, nutty finish.

It is on the list for nuts and coffee. Its flavors are the coffee cake’s own: chicory coffee, bittersweet chocolate, pecans and spiced citrus glaze.

value.a:
Asked: What is a Colheita?

Answer: A tawny Port from a single harvest, aged for many years in cask before bottling; ours is from 1997.

Asked: How is it different from vintage Port?

Answer: Vintage Port ages mostly in bottle and stays dark and fruity; a Colheita ages in cask and turns amber, nutty and silky.

Asked: Does it need decanting?

Answer: No, a tawny has no sediment, so we pour it straight from the bottle.

value.a:
Grgich Hills Violetta 2012 is a late harvest Napa dessert wine in a half-bottle, $145 for 375 ml, filed under Dessert Wines, United States, and the half-bottle for World Famous Bananas Foster.

Grgich Hills Estate, in Rutherford in the Napa Valley, was founded by Mike Grgich, the winemaker behind the Chateau Montelena Chardonnay that won the Paris tasting of 1976; our list carries Montelena too. Violetta is its rare dessert wine, made only in a handful of years, when noble rot shrivels Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling and a little Gewürztraminer in its low-lying American Canyon vineyard.

The guest sees a half-bottle, about four small dessert pours. In the glass it is deep gold. It tastes of dried peach, candied orange, honey and sweet flowers, rich and luscious, with fresh acidity.

It is on the list for our most famous dessert. Its sweetness carries the brown sugar and rum caramel of Bananas Foster and the vanilla ice cream.

Joseph Phelps Insignia 2011 is a famous Napa red in a half-bottle, $240 for 375 ml, filed under Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, and our anchor among the red half-bottles.

Joseph Phelps Vineyards is in St. Helena, in the Napa Valley. Insignia was first made in 1974, one of California’s first proprietary blends in the Bordeaux style, named rather than labeled by grape, and it is still the winery’s flagship. It is Cabernet Sauvignon-led with other Bordeaux grapes; the blend of the 2011 is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is deep garnet with some bricking at the rim. With more than a decade of age it tastes of blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and dried herbs, its tannin softened, savory and long.

It is on the list for a guest who wants a great Napa name without a full bottle. It suits the Chateaubriand and the filet.

Keller PIUS Auslese 2022 is a sweet Rheinhessen wine in a half-bottle, $245 for 375 ml, filed under German Riesling, Rheinhessen, and the half-bottle for the Pineapple Tarte Tatin.

Weingut Keller is a family estate in Flörsheim-Dalsheim in Rheinhessen, and one of the most admired growers in Germany for its dry Rieslings. PIUS is its sweet Auslese, blended from late harvest and botrytis-touched grapes. Although the list files it with Riesling, the varieties change with the vintage; which ones are in the 2022 is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a half-bottle, about four small dessert pours. In the glass it is deep gold. It tastes of honeyed apricot, pineapple and spice, rich and pure, held up by a stony acidity.

It is on the list for tropical fruit and caramel. With the charred pineapple, the fruit matches, and the acidity keeps the puff pastry and the anglaise light.

value.a:
Château d’Yquem 2015 is the most famous sweet wine in the world, in a half-bottle, $450 for 375 ml, filed under Dessert Wines, France, and the celebration choice for the Framboise French toast.

Château d’Yquem, in Sauternes, is the only estate ranked Premier Cru Supérieur, above every other Sauternes, in the 1855 classification. Its pickers pass through the vineyard many times each harvest, taking only the berries that noble rot has shriveled, and in poor years no Yquem is made at all. It is Sémillon-led with Sauvignon Blanc.

The guest sees a half-bottle, about four small pours. In the glass it is deep gold. The 2015 tastes of apricot, candied orange, saffron, honey and vanilla, luminous and luscious, with fresh acidity and a very long finish.

It is on the list for the grand celebration. With the French toast, its richness meets the mascarpone and the raspberry coulis.

Answer: It is the only Sauternes ranked above all others in 1855, and it is picked berry by berry; in poor years none is made.

value.a:
Mas de Valériole Vé 2025 is a Mediterranean rosé in a magnum, $85 for 1.5 L, under Large Formats, Rosé, and the gentlest priced big bottle on our list.

Mas de Valériole is a family estate in the Camargue, the delta south of Arles where the Rhône meets the sea, and its vineyards are cooled by the steady Mediterranean wind. Vé is a Provençal expression meaning look at that. The rosé blends Caladoc, a cross of Grenache and Malbec, with Merlot and Marselan, pressed straight off the skins and kept fresh in steel tanks.

The guest sees a magnum, twice the size of a standard bottle, about ten to twelve glasses. In the glass it is very pale pink. It tastes of raspberry and ripe citrus with a salty, sea breeze finish, light and dry.

It is on the list for a party that is sharing. A magnum of rosé on the table says summer, and it suits the tomato tostada, the crab claws and the Roost Bar snacks.

value.a:
Jean Foillard Morgon Côte du Py 2023 is a cru Beaujolais in a magnum, $250 for 1.5 L, under Large Formats, Red, France.

Jean Foillard is a grower in Morgon, one of the ten crus of Beaujolais, and one of the four growers, with Marcel Lapierre, Guy Breton and Jean-Paul Thévenet, who led the region back to traditional methods: whole bunches, native yeasts and a light hand in the cellar. The Côte du Py is the famous hill above Morgon, of old volcanic schist, and its Gamay is deeper and more structured than most Beaujolais.

The guest sees a magnum, about ten to twelve glasses. In the glass it is a deep, bright ruby. It tastes of dark cherry, raspberry and violet with a mineral, earthy depth, silky tannin and lively acidity.

It is on the list as the red for a table ordering a bit of everything. It is light enough for the redfish and deep enough for the duck.

value.a:
Château Cos d’Estournel 2015 is a Second Growth Saint-Estèphe in a magnum, $600 for 1.5 L, under Large Formats, Red, France.

Cos d’Estournel is in Saint-Estèphe, in the Médoc on Bordeaux’s Left Bank, and was ranked a Second Growth in the 1855 classification. Its founder traded with India and built the château’s famous pagoda towers. The wine is Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot; the 2015 blend is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a magnum, two bottles in one, decanted at the side stand. In the glass it is deep purple garnet. It tastes of blackcurrant, plum, cedar and cocoa with a touch of exotic spice, powerful and polished, with fine tannin and a long finish.

It is on the list as a grand Bordeaux for a party. A magnum ages slowly and gracefully, and it suits the Chateaubriand and the filet.

Joh. Jos. Prüm is the most famous estate of Wehlen on the Mosel, run by the Prüm family, and the Wehlener Sonnenuhr is its great steep vineyard of blue slate, named for the sundial built into the slope. GKA stands for Goldkapsel Auslese: a sweet, selected harvest, and the gold capsule marks richer fruit.

The guest sees a magnum, enough for about twenty small dessert pours. In the glass it is gold. It tastes of honeyed pineapple, apricot, lime and slate, sweet and racy, light in alcohol, and Prüm’s wines are known for aging for decades.

It is on the list for a big table sharing dessert. Its pineapple meets the charred pineapple of the tatin.

Billecart-Salmon Réserve in a Nebuchadnezzar is the largest bottle on our list, $4900 for 15 L, printed under Champagne, Grande Marques.

A Nebuchadnezzar holds fifteen liters, the same as twenty standard bottles, and ours is filled with Billecart-Salmon Réserve, the house Brut of the family house in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, founded in 1818: Meunier, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with reserve wines, in a fresh, delicate style.

The guest sees a bottle taller than a child, opened and poured as a performance. It pours a hundred glasses or more. In the glass it is pale gold with fine bubbles and tastes of pear, citrus and a light brioche.

It is on the list for a private event, a wedding party or a very large celebration. It needs planning: it is ordered ahead, chilled for hours in a large tub of ice and water, and opened and poured by the sommelier with a second person, often from a cradle. The same wine comes in a 750 ml bottle and a magnum.

value.a:
Louis Michel Chablis 2022 is the village Chablis on our list, $80, filed under Burgundy white, Chablis, and the value bottle for the redfish Véronique.

Domaine Louis Michel is a family estate in Chablis, the northernmost part of Burgundy, where the cool climate and the chalky clay soils give Chardonnay a lean, mineral style. The estate is known for making every wine in steel tanks with no oak at all, so the wine tastes of the place rather than the barrel. Our list also carries its Premier Cru Montmains in a half-bottle.

In the glass it is pale with a green tint. It tastes of green apple, lemon and white flowers, crisp and precise, with a chalky, oyster-shell finish.

It is on the list as the classic fish white at a value price. Its acidity matches the preserved lemon and the hibiscus-pickled grapes of the redfish, and its texture holds up to the beurre blanc.

value.a:
Domaine du Roc des Boutires En Bertilionne 2020 is a single parcel Pouilly-Fuissé, $90, filed under Burgundy white, Mâconnais, and the value bottle for the Louisiana crab claws.

Pouilly-Fuissé is the best known appellation of the Mâconnais, in southern Burgundy, where vineyards spread beneath the great limestone rock of Solutré. Domaine du Roc des Boutires has been owned since 2016 by the Parinet family, who also own Château du Moulin-à-Vent in Beaujolais. En Bertilionne is a small east-facing parcel of older Chardonnay vines in the heart of Pouilly, facing the rock.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of ripe lemon, white flowers and hay, round and textured, with a saline, pithy finish, and the 2020 has a few years of bottle age.

It is on the list as white Burgundy with real character under $100. With the crab claws, its roundness meets the brown butter vinaigrette and its acidity keeps the sweet crab fresh.

value.a:
Jean-Philippe Fichet Bourgogne Blanc 2023 is a white Burgundy from a Meursault grower, $95, filed under Burgundy white, Bourgogne, and the value bottle for the Louisiana BBQ lobster.

Jean-Philippe Fichet is a grower in Meursault, the Côte de Beaune village famous for rich, nutty white Burgundy. Bourgogne Blanc is the regional appellation, Chardonnay that may come from vineyards outside the famous villages, and in a good grower’s hands it carries the house style. How it is aged is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of lemon and white peach with a hint of hazelnut, creamy in texture with fresh acidity.

It is on the list as our white Burgundy anchor under $100. With the BBQ lobster, its texture meets the butter and the sweet meat, and its freshness clears the spicy nduja and the white bean stew.

Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine 2023 is a Mâconnais white, $100, filed under Burgundy white, Mâconnais, and the sweet spot bottle for the crab and corn omelette.

The Lafon family of Domaine des Comtes Lafon in Meursault are among the great names of white Burgundy; their Clos de la Baronne is also on our list. Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon is the family’s estate in the Mâconnais, in southern Burgundy, and this wine comes from vines around the village of Milly-Lamartine.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of pear, lemon and white flowers, round and ripe, with a chalky freshness and a clean, bright finish.

It is on the list as a great Burgundy name at a friendly price. With the crab and corn omelette, its round fruit meets the roasted sweet corn and the miso butter, and its freshness answers the lemon, the basil and the Marcona almond gremolata.

Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé 2021 is the full bottle of the white we pour by Coravin, $160, filed under Burgundy white, Mâconnais, and the sweet spot bottle for the redfish Véronique.

Domaine Leflaive is the great estate of Puligny-Montrachet, one of the most famous names in white Burgundy. In the Mâconnais, in southern Burgundy, it farms vines in the village of Verzé, and this is the wine they make, all Chardonnay. Our list carries Leflaive’s Puligny, its Meursault Premier Cru and its Chevalier-Montrachet as well.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of lemon, white peach and a touch of hazelnut, with a silky texture, a chalky line and precise acidity.

By the glass we pour the 2022 through the Coravin; the full bottle on the list is the 2021. With the redfish, its texture holds up to the beurre blanc and its citrus meets the preserved lemon.

value.a:
Jean-Paul and Benoît Droin Vaillons 2023 is a Chablis Premier Cru, $175, filed under Burgundy white, Chablis Premier Cru, and our anchor between village and Grand Cru Chablis.

Jean-Paul and Benoît Droin are a father and son family estate in Chablis, the northernmost part of Burgundy. Vaillons is one of the best known Premier Cru slopes of Chablis, on the left bank of the Serein river. How the family ages it, in steel or partly in oak, is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is pale gold with a green tint. It tastes of lemon, green apple and white flowers, with a chalky, saline depth, crisp and precise, a little fuller than village Chablis.

It is on the list as the Chablis for a guest who wants more than the village wine without the Grand Cru price. It suits the Grand Isle oysters, the redfish and the crab claws.

value.a:
Raymond Dupont-Fahn Meursault Les Tillets 2022 is a village Meursault from a high single site, $175, filed under Burgundy white, Meursault, and the sweet spot bottle for the Louisiana BBQ lobster.

Domaine Dupont-Fahn is a family estate in Tailly, just south of Meursault, now run by Raymond Dupont-Fahn. Les Tillets is a lieu-dit, a named vineyard, near the top of the village slope, one of the highest in Meursault, stony limestone named for its linden trees. It is not classed Premier Cru, but its altitude gives the wine an unusual freshness.

In the glass it is gold. It tastes of lemon, hazelnut and toast, rich and nutty in the Meursault way, with a stony, electric freshness running through it.

It is on the list as Meursault at a sweet spot price. With the BBQ lobster, its richness matches the sweet meat and the butter, and the freshness keeps the white bean stew and the nduja lively.

Domaine Paul Pillot Le Charmois 2022 is a Saint-Aubin Premier Cru, $215, filed under Burgundy white, Saint-Aubin Premier Cru, and the sweet spot bottle for the Louisiana crab claws.

Domaine Paul Pillot is a family estate in Chassagne-Montrachet, in the Côte de Beaune. Saint-Aubin is the hillside village tucked behind Puligny and Chassagne, and its best slopes are rated Premier Cru; Le Charmois is one of them, close to the boundary with Puligny. White Burgundy lovers know Saint-Aubin as the place to find the Puligny style at a gentler price.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of lemon, white peach and toasted hazelnut, with a chalky snap and bright acidity.

It is on the list as a Premier Cru in the sweet spot. With the crab claws, its nutty notes meet the warm brown butter vinaigrette, and its chalk and acidity keep the sweet crab and fines herbes fresh.

The Carillon family has farmed vines there for centuries; in 2010 the estate was divided between two brothers, and François Carillon set up his own domaine.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of citrus, white peach, toasted hazelnut and a little smoke, elegant and precise, with Puligny’s fine, chalky tension and a long finish.

It is on the list as Puligny from a classic grower family. With the crab claws, its toasty, nutty depth mirrors the brown butter vinaigrette and lifts the fines herbes, while its tension keeps the sweet crab fresh.

value.a:
Domaine René et Vincent Dauvissat Les Preuses 2015 is a Chablis Grand Cru with bottle age, $350, filed under Chablis Grand Cru, and the celebration bottle for the Grand Isle Jewel oysters.

Dauvissat is a family domaine in Chablis and, with Raveneau, one of the two great reference estates of the region. Les Preuses is one of the seven Grand Cru slopes rising above the town of Chablis. Dauvissat ages its wines partly in old oak barrels, which adds texture without the taste of new wood.

In the glass it is gold with a green glint. The 2015 tastes of lemon peel, white flowers and oyster shell with a touch of honey from age, steely and precise, with deep, saline length.

It is on the list as the grandest form of the classic pairing. Chablis and oysters share a briny, mineral character, and with the Grand Isle oysters its steel meets the brine while its depth stands up to the Fresno chili mignonette.

Sous le Dos d’Ane means under the donkey’s back, for the shape of the hill. It is a Premier Cru of Meursault lying right on the boundary with Puligny-Montrachet, and Domaine Leflaive, the most famous estate of Puligny, farms it. So it is Meursault made by Puligny hands: richer than Leflaive’s Puligny wines, finer than much of the village.

In the glass it is gold. The 2017 tastes layered and toasty: lemon, hazelnut, brioche and a little smoke, with a long finish.

It is on the list for the grandest lobster course. Its toasty depth meets the roasted lobster and the smoky nduja, and its freshness keeps the white bean stew bright.
