value.a:
Domaine Roulot Meursault 2022 is a village Meursault from a cult estate, $500, filed under Burgundy white, Meursault, and an anchor among the great names on our list.

Domaine Roulot is a family estate in Meursault, run by Jean-Marc Roulot. His taut, precise wines changed how many people think of Meursault, a village long known for rich, buttery white Burgundy. Even the village wine is allocated and hard to find.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes taut and precise rather than buttery: lemon, green apple and white flowers with a stony, saline finish, and the village’s depth underneath.

It is on the list because collectors ask for it and because it shows the other face of Meursault. It suits pure seafood, the crab claws, the redfish and the oysters, and its precision makes it lovely with the lobster.

Domaine Coche-Dury Bourgogne Blanc 2022 is the regional white of the most sought after white Burgundy estate, $690, filed under Burgundy white, Bourgogne.

Domaine Coche-Dury is a family estate in Meursault, now run by Raphaël Coche after his father, Jean-François Coche-Dury. Its wines are among the scarcest and most collected in the world. Bourgogne Blanc is the regional appellation, the humblest label in Burgundy, but Coche-Dury makes it with the same care as its Grand Cru, which is why the bottle is priced far above any other Bourgogne.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes flinty and reductive: lemon, hazelnut and a struck-match note, taut and long.

It is on the list for the collector who wants a taste of the estate. Pour it with simple, pure seafood, the crab claws, the redfish or the oysters, so nothing hides it.

value.a:
Domaine François Raveneau Montée de Tonnerre 2022 is a cult Chablis Premier Cru, $920, filed under Chablis Premier Cru.

Raveneau is a family domaine in Chablis and, with Dauvissat, one of the two great reference estates of the region. Its wines are allocated and among the hardest to find in Burgundy. Montée de Tonnerre is one of the finest Premier Crus, on the right bank of the Serein beside the Grand Crus, and Raveneau ages it in old barrels.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes intense and taut: lemon, white flowers, oyster shell and a smoky, stony depth, with Grand Cru power in a Premier Cru.

It is on the list because collectors ask for it by name. Young Raveneau can be tight, so the sommelier may decant it. It is grand with the Grand Isle oysters, the crab claws and the redfish.

Chevalier-Montrachet is a Grand Cru in Puligny-Montrachet, on the steep, stony slope just above Le Montrachet, the most famous white wine vineyard in the world. Domaine Leflaive, the great estate of Puligny, is one of its most famous owners; our list also carries its village Puligny and its Mâcon-Verzé.

In the glass it is bright gold. The 2015 tastes stony and powerful: lemon curd, white flowers, hazelnut and a smoky mineral depth, with layers that keep unfolding long after each sip.

It is on the list for the collector and the grandest occasion. Serve it barely chilled in a large glass so it can open, and let the sommelier lead. It belongs with the BBQ lobster or the crab claws.

value.a:
Château d’Esclans Whispering Angel 2024 is the best known Provence rosé on our list, $50, filed under Rosé, France, and the value bottle for the Creole tomato tostada.

Château d’Esclans is an estate in the hills of Provence, inland from the Riviera, and Whispering Angel is the pale rosé that helped make Provence rosé fashionable in America. It is Grenache-led with Cinsault and Rolle, pressed gently so the juice takes only a blush of color. By the glass we pour another Provence rosé, the Minuty Prestige.

In the glass it is very pale pink. It tastes of white peach, wild strawberry and citrus zest, dry and refreshing, with a light mineral finish.

It is on the list because guests ask for it by name, and it suits our late summer plates. Tomatoes are high in acid, and a dry rosé matches them, while its delicacy leaves the creamy burrata alone.

Loimer Lois Grüner Veltliner 2022 is a light Austrian white, $55, filed under Austria and Hungary, Kamptal, and the value bottle for the Eggs Sardou.

Loimer is an estate in Langenlois, in the Kamptal region northwest of Vienna, run by Fred Loimer. Grüner Veltliner is Austria’s own white grape, known for a note of white pepper, and Lois is the estate’s fresh, everyday bottling.

In the glass it is pale green gold. It tastes of green apple, lime and white pepper with a green herbal note, light, crisp and dry.

It is on the list for green flavors at a value price. Artichokes make most wines taste sweet or metallic, but Grüner stays itself, and its peppery freshness cuts the Parmesan creamed spinach and the Choron sauce of the Sardou. It is also lovely with the Creole Caesar.

value.a:
Stein Weihwasser Feinherb 2023 is an off dry Mosel Riesling, $55, filed under German Riesling, Mosel, and the value bottle for the seafood gumbo.

Weingut Stein is a small estate in the village of Alf on the Mosel, run by Ulrich Stein, who has spent years rescuing steep slate vineyards others abandoned. Weihwasser means holy water: the old vines grow on slate near the old church. Feinherb means just off dry, and the wine ferments in large old casks.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of Asian pear, lime and lychee with a salty lemon note, a touch of sweetness balancing crisp acidity.

It is on the list for spice at a value price. A touch of sweetness cools heat, so it calms the andouille in the gumbo, and its acidity lifts the dark roux and freshens the seafood.

value.a:
Stein Palmberg-Terrassen Spätlese-Feinherb 2014 is an aged, off dry Mosel Riesling, $62, filed under German Riesling, Mosel, and the value bottle for the duck confit waffle.

It comes from Ulrich Stein’s small estate on the Mosel, the same grower as our Weihwasser, from the terraced Palmberg vineyard. Spätlese means late picked, riper grapes than a Kabinett, and feinherb means the wine is finished just off dry rather than sweet. The 2014 has had years in bottle.

In the glass it is deep gold. It tastes of baked apple, apricot and honey, with the petrol note aged Riesling develops, and juicy acidity keeps it lively.

It is on the list as an aged Riesling at a value price. With the duck confit waffle, its touch of sweetness meets the mustard maple syrup, and its acidity cuts the duck fat and the foie gras butter.

value.a:
Domaine de l’Écu Orthogneiss 2022 is a serious Muscadet, $70, filed under Loire white, Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine, and the value bottle for the Creole Caesar.

Domaine de l’Écu is an estate in Le Landreau, near Nantes, where the Loire meets the Atlantic. Muscadet is made from the Melon de Bourgogne grape, and this estate bottles each wine by the rock its vines grow on. Orthogneiss is a hard, ancient metamorphic rock, and the wine ages for a long time on its lees, the spent yeast, which adds texture and savory depth.

In the glass it is pale straw. It tastes of lemon, green apple and crushed stone with a salty, savory depth, bone dry and more textured than most Muscadet.

It is on the list for salt and the sea. With the Caesar, its salinity matches the smoked oyster dressing and its acidity cuts the Grana Padano and the Leidenheimer crisps.

value.a:
Domaine de la Pépière Monnières-Saint Fiacre 2020 is a cru Muscadet, $75, filed under Loire white, Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine, and the value bottle for the Grand Isle Jewel oysters.

Muscadet is made from the Melon de Bourgogne grape near Nantes, where the Loire meets the Atlantic, and it is the classic French oyster wine. Domaine de la Pépière, founded by Marc Ollivier, is one of the reference estates. Monnières-Saint Fiacre is one of the crus communaux, the top villages of Muscadet, whose wines must age for a long time on their lees before release.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of lemon, green apple, sea spray and crushed shells, bone dry and saline, with more depth and texture than a young Muscadet.

It is on the list for raw oysters. Its salt and acidity mirror the brine and the mignonette vinegar, and it stays calm beside the Fresno chili.

value.a:
Sandhi Chardonnay Sta. Rita Hills 2021 is a cool climate California white, $75, filed under United States Chardonnay, Central Coast, and the value bottle for the pecan Gulf fish.

Sandhi is a Santa Barbara County winery founded by the sommelier Rajat Parr with the winemaker Sashi Moorman, known for fresh, restrained wines. The Sta. Rita Hills is a cool appellation close to the Pacific, where ocean fog and wind keep Chardonnay bright.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of lemon, white peach and a little hazelnut, fresh but creamy, with bright acidity: California fruit in a Burgundian style.

It is on the list for the guest who likes Chardonnay but not a heavy one. With the pecan Gulf fish, its texture meets the lump crab and the cauliflower purée, and its acidity keeps the flaky fish light against the pecan bordelaise.

value.a:
Trimbach Riesling Réserve 2020 is a dry Alsace Riesling, $85, filed under Alsace white, Riesling, and our anchor among the dry Rieslings.

F.E. Trimbach is a family house in Ribeauvillé, in Alsace, the French region along the Rhine facing Germany, and the same family has run it for centuries. Trimbach is famous for bone dry, long-lived Riesling, and its Clos Sainte Hune and Réserve Personnelle Pinot Gris are also on our list. The Réserve is the house’s classic Riesling.

In the glass it is pale straw. It tastes of lime, green apple and white flowers with a stony, steely finish, bone dry, crisp and taut.

It is on the list as the reference for dry Riesling. Guests often expect Riesling to be sweet; Alsace Riesling from Trimbach is the opposite. It suits the gumbo, the crab claws and the shrimp and grits.

value.a:
Huet Le Haut-Lieu Sec 2024 is a young dry Vouvray, $90, filed under Loire white, Vouvray and Touraine, and the value bottle for the Louisiana oysters.

Domaine Huet is one of the great estates of Vouvray, on the Loire near Tours, and it grows only Chenin Blanc in three vineyards. Le Haut-Lieu is where the estate began, and Sec means dry. The same wine from 2019 is on our list in a half-bottle, a few years older.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of quince, pear, lemon and white flowers, textured and dry, with bright, juicy acidity and a chalky finish.

It is on the list as a sommelier’s white at a value price. With the barbecue oysters, its texture holds up to the buttery, peppery sauce, and its acidity cuts the pickled collard greens and shallots.

value.a:
Au Bon Climat Sanford & Benedict 2021 is a single vineyard California Chardonnay, $95, filed under United States Chardonnay, Central Coast, and the value bottle for the Poussin à la Moutarde.

Au Bon Climat was founded in Santa Barbara County by the late Jim Clendenen, a pioneer who made California Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in a Burgundian style. Sanford & Benedict is one of the oldest vineyards of the Sta. Rita Hills, a cool appellation near the Pacific.

In the glass it is gold. It tastes of lemon curd, pear and hazelnut with a little toast, rich but fresh, with bright acidity.

It is on the list as a classic California Chardonnay under $100. With the poussin, its richness mirrors the mustard cream sauce, and its acidity cuts the sweet tea-brined, fried crust and the turnips.

value.a:
Kumeu River Estate Chardonnay 2022 is a New Zealand Chardonnay, $95, filed under International White, New Zealand, and the value bottle for the crab and corn omelette.

Kumeu River is a family winery near Auckland, on New Zealand’s North Island, run by the Brajkovich family and famous above all for its Chardonnay, which is often compared with white Burgundy. The Estate is blended from the family’s own vineyards around Kumeu.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of lemon, white peach and hazelnut, with a gentle creaminess, bright acidity and a fine, mineral finish.

It is on the list as one of the great Chardonnays of the southern hemisphere under $100, and a conversation piece. With the omelette, its gentle richness meets the lump crab and the house-made miso butter, and its citrus answers the lemon and basil.

value.a:
Albert Boxler Pinot Gris 2020 is a rich Alsace white, $110, filed under Alsace white, Pinot Gris, and the sweet spot bottle for the duck confit waffle.

Albert Boxler is a small family domaine in Niedermorschwihr, a village in the hills above Colmar in Alsace, known for intense, precise wines that collectors seek out. Pinot Gris in Alsace is a different wine from Italian Pinot Grigio: richer, fuller and more aromatic. Whether this bottling carries a touch of sweetness is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is a deep gold. It tastes of ripe pear, quince, honey and smoke with a gentle spice, rich and full, balanced by acidity.

It is on the list for duck and foie gras. In Alsace, Pinot Gris with foie gras is a classic pairing, and it stands up to the Rohan duck leg confit, the foie gras butter and the mustard maple syrup.

value.a:
Gaia Wild Ferment Assyrtiko 2023 is a volcanic island white from Greece, $110, filed under Italy and Greece, White, Greece, and the sweet spot bottle for the Gulf fish en papillote.

Gaia Wines makes Assyrtiko on Santorini, a volcanic island in the Aegean. Its vines grow low to the ground, trained into basket shapes to shelter the grapes from the wind, in soils of volcanic ash and pumice. Assyrtiko is the island’s great white grape, known for keeping high acidity in a hot climate. Wild Ferment means it is fermented with native yeasts.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of lemon, salt, flint and white flowers, bone dry, with piercing acidity and a textured, savory depth.

It is on the list as our anchor from Greece. With the papillote, its salty, lemony acidity meets the Castelvetrano olives and tomato, and its texture suits the crab and Gulf fish.

value.a:
Domaine Tempier Bandol Rosé 2024 is one of the great rosés of France, $120, filed under Rosé, France, and the sweet spot bottle for the Creole tomato tostada.

Domaine Tempier is the reference estate of Bandol, a small appellation on the Provençal coast between Marseille and Toulon, run for generations by the Peyraud family. Bandol is the home of the Mourvèdre grape, and Tempier’s rosé is Mourvèdre-led with Grenache and Cinsault.

In the glass it is pale salmon. It tastes of wild strawberry, blood orange and garrigue herbs, dry, with a savory, saline depth and more body than most rosé; it can even age a few years.

It is on the list as the serious rosé. With the tostada, its body stands up to the smoked tomato water and the housemade okra tostada, and its acidity matches the heirloom tomatoes and burrata.

value.a:
J.J. Prüm Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett 2020 is a classic Mosel Riesling, $135, filed under German Riesling, Mosel, and the sweet spot bottle for the seafood gumbo.

Joh. Jos. Prüm is the most famous estate of Wehlen on the Mosel, and the Wehlener Sonnenuhr is its great steep vineyard of blue slate, named for the sundial built into the slope; the Prüm Auslese in magnum is also on our list. Kabinett is the lightest of Germany’s ripeness levels, and Prüm’s Kabinett is lightly sweet and low in alcohol.

In the glass it is pale, sometimes with a little spritz when young. It tastes of green apple, peach, lime and slate, delicate and racy.

It is on the list as the Kabinett from a legendary name. A touch of sweetness soothes the andouille’s spice, and its racy acidity refreshes after the dark roux and the seafood.

value.a:
Huet Clos du Bourg Demi-Sec 2015 is an aged, gently sweet Vouvray, $145, filed under Loire white, Vouvray and Touraine, and a first pick for the cheese board.

Domaine Huet is one of the great estates of Vouvray, on the Loire near Tours, and the Clos du Bourg is a walled vineyard in the heart of the village, one of its three. Demi-sec means half dry, gently sweet. Chenin Blanc ages beautifully, and the 2015 has a decade in bottle.

In the glass it is a deep gold. It tastes of honey, quince, baked apple, beeswax and chamomile, gently sweet, held up by bright acidity.

It is on the list for cheese and honey. Sweetness flatters salty cheese, the Brennan’s honey on the board echoes the wine, and the acidity cuts through the richness and the fruit and nut bread.

value.a:
Bründlmayer Alte Reben Grüner Veltliner 2023 is an old vine Austrian white, $150, filed under Austria and Hungary, Kamptal, and the sweet spot bottle for the Eggs Sardou.

Bründlmayer is the leading family estate of Langenlois, in Austria’s Kamptal, and our list carries its Terrassen Grüner and its Heiligenstein Riesling in half-bottles. Alte Reben means old vines: older vines give smaller crops and deeper, more concentrated wine.

In the glass it is gold. It tastes of ripe pear, citrus and white pepper with a savory note, fuller and more textured than a classic Grüner, dry, with a long finish.

It is on the list as the deeper side of Austria’s grape. Like every Grüner it handles artichokes, which upset most wines, and its texture holds up to the Choron sauce and the Parmesan creamed spinach of the Sardou.

White Bordeaux blends Sauvignon Blanc, for freshness, with Sémillon, for body and texture; Carbonnieux ages its white in barrel.

It is on the list as Albariño at its grandest. With the Caesar, its saline citrus meets the smoked oyster dressing and cuts the Grana Padano.

Chateau Montelena Chardonnay 2023 is the Napa Chardonnay with the most famous story, $175, filed under United States Chardonnay, Napa Valley, and the sweet spot bottle for the pecan Gulf fish.

Chateau Montelena is in Calistoga, at the north end of the Napa Valley. At the Paris tasting of 1976, French judges tasting blind ranked its 1973 Chardonnay above the great white Burgundies, and California wine was taken seriously from that day. The winemaker then was Mike Grgich, whose Violetta is on our list.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of green apple, lemon and pear with a little toast, balanced and restrained, with bright acidity, less buttery than many Napa Chardonnays.

It is on the list for its story and its balance. With the pecan fish, it has the richness for the pecan bordelaise and the freshness for the lump crab.

value.a:
Domaine de Trévallon Blanc 2016 is a rare white from Provence, $265, filed under France, Other White, Provence, and the celebration bottle for the Gulf fish en papillote.

Domaine de Trévallon is a family estate in the Alpilles, the limestone hills near Les Baux in Provence. It is famous for making wine its own way: its blends fall outside the rules of the local appellation, so the label carries the broader Alpilles name. The white is made in tiny amounts, Marsanne-led with Roussanne, Chardonnay and a little Grenache Blanc and Clairette; the mix changes by vintage.

In the glass it is a deep gold. The 2016 tastes of apricot, white flowers, honey and fennel with Provençal herbs, rich and textured, with a fresh, stony finish.

It is on the list as a rarity for a celebration. With the papillote, its herbs echo the olives, tomato and banana leaf.

value.a:
Pascal Cotat Lot 2024 is a rare Pinot Noir rosé from Chavignol, $270, filed under Rosé, France, and the celebration bottle for the Creole tomato tostada.

Pascal Cotat is a family grower in Chavignol, a village of Sancerre famous for steep chalk slopes; his Les Monts Damnés Sancerre is also on our list. The rosé comes from a tiny parcel of Pinot Noir the family has farmed for decades. A local dispute took the parcel out of the Sancerre appellation, so it is labeled more simply and by lot, here Lot 2024, rather than by vintage.

In the glass it is a pale copper pink. It tastes of wild strawberry, red currant and crushed chalk, dry and taut, with more structure than most rosé.

It is on the list as a cult rarity. With the tostada, its chalky acidity meets the heirloom and Creole tomatoes, and its red fruit sits beside the burrata.

value.a:
Kongsgaard Chardonnay Napa Valley 2016 is a cult California white with bottle age, $280, filed under United States Chardonnay, Napa Valley, and the celebration bottle for the pecan Gulf fish.

Kongsgaard is the family winery of John Kongsgaard, a Napa winemaker whose Chardonnays are among the most sought after in California. They are made in small amounts in a rich, long-aging style; how this one is made and aged is a question for the sommelier. The 2016 has had years in bottle.

In the glass it is a deep gold. It tastes of lemon curd, baked pear, hazelnut and honey with a smoky, savory depth, rich and layered yet fresh, with a very long finish.

It is on the list for the Chardonnay collector. With the pecan fish, its power stands up to the pecan bordelaise and the lump crab, and it is grand with the BBQ lobster.

value.a:
Franz Hirtzberger Honivogl Smaragd 2022 is a grand Austrian Grüner Veltliner, $320, filed under Austria and Hungary, Wachau, and the celebration bottle for the Eggs Sardou.

Franz Hirtzberger is a family estate in Spitz, at the western end of the Wachau, the steep, terraced Danube valley that makes Austria’s greatest dry whites. Honivogl is its most famous Grüner Veltliner vineyard. Smaragd, named for the emerald lizards that sun themselves on the terraces, is the Wachau’s ripest category of dry wine.

In the glass it is gold. It tastes of ripe pear, quince and white pepper with honeyed spice and stone, rich and powerful yet dry, with a long finish.

It is on the list as Grüner Veltliner at its grandest. With the Sardou, it has the weight for the Parmesan creamed spinach and the Choron sauce, and like every Grüner it is at ease with artichoke.

Les Monts Damnés, the damned mountains, is the steep chalk slope above the village, so steep it is worked by hand. Cotat picks his Sauvignon Blanc ripe, and the wines are built to age.

value.a:
F.E. Trimbach Pinot Gris Réserve Personnelle 2007 is a top Alsace Pinot Gris with long bottle age, $360, filed under Alsace white, Pinot Gris, and the celebration bottle for the duck confit waffle.

Trimbach is the family house of Ribeauvillé in Alsace, famous for long-lived whites; its Riesling Réserve and its Clos Sainte Hune are also on our list. Réserve Personnelle is the house’s top bottling of Pinot Gris, made from its best vineyards; which ones, and how much sweetness the 2007 carries, are questions for the sommelier.

value.a:
Domaine du Pélican Vin Jaune 2016 is the great rarity of the Jura, $655, filed under France, Other White, Savoie and Jura, and the celebration bottle for the turtle soup.

Domaine du Pélican is an estate in Arbois, in the Jura mountains of eastern France, founded by the d’Angerville family of Volnay in Burgundy. Vin Jaune, yellow wine, is made from the Savagnin grape and aged at least six years in barrel without topping up, under a veil of yeast that forms on the surface, much as fino sherry ages under flor. It is traditionally sold in a small bottle called a clavelin.

In the glass it is a deep yellow gold. It tastes of walnut, curry spice, dried apple and almond, with a salty, savory tang, dry, powerful and endless.

value.a:
Château Haut-Brion Blanc 2019 is one of the rarest white wines in the world, $2500, filed under France, Other White, Bordeaux.

Château Haut-Brion is in Pessac, on the edge of the city of Bordeaux, in the appellation of Pessac-Léognan. In the 1855 classification it was the one estate outside the Médoc ranked a First Growth for its red. Its white is made in tiny amounts from Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc and is counted among the greatest dry whites anywhere, built to age for decades.

In the glass it is gold. The 2019 tastes of lemon curd, white peach, beeswax and toasted almond with a smoky, stony depth, rich yet precise, with immense length.

It is on the list for the collector and the grandest occasion; the sommelier should lead. It belongs with the BBQ lobster, the crab claws or the redfish, the richest seafood of the house.

value.a:
Domaine Coudert's Clos de la Roilette Fleurie 2023 is the value bottle with our New Orleans Shrimp & Grits: bin 34574, $65 on the bottle list.

Fleurie, fluh-REE, is one of the ten crus of Beaujolais, the top villages at the south end of Burgundy, and the grape is Gamay. Clos de la Roilette is a single walled vineyard the Coudert family farm in Fleurie, where it meets Moulin-à-Vent. How long it rests and in what vessel is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is bright ruby with a purple edge. It tastes of red cherry, raspberry and violet, light in body, with soft tannin and fresh acidity, and it drinks well young.

It is on this list because tomato and spice are hard on big reds. Low tannin will not turn bitter against the Creole sauce, and served lightly chilled it stays fresh beside the tasso and the fried pimento cheese grit cake. For a guest who wants red at brunch, it is the easy yes.

The Faiveley Bourgogne Rouge 2022 is our value red Burgundy and the value bottle with the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast: bin 22651, $90.

Faiveley, fev-LAY, is a family wine house in Nuits-Saint-Georges, in the Côte de Nuits, with vineyards across the Côte d'Or and the Côte Chalonnaise. Bourgogne, boor-GOHN-yuh, is the regional name: Pinot Noir drawn from vineyards across Burgundy rather than one village, so it shows the grape more than a place.

In the glass it is a clear, bright ruby. It tastes of bright cherry and red currant, light to medium in body, with fresh acidity and fine tannin.

That acidity cuts the richness of duck, and the red fruit meets the cane syrup peaches, so it is the classic match at a fair price. The list prints it twice, on the Burgundy pages and on Selections Under $100, under the same bin, which makes it the easiest red Burgundy to find and to recommend.

value.a:
Marcel Lapierre's Morgon 2023 is the value bottle with the Eggs Owen: bin 289213, $95.

Lapierre, lah-PYAIR, is a family estate in Villié-Morgon in Beaujolais. Marcel Lapierre was one of a small group of growers who led the region back to old ways of making Gamay: whole bunches, native yeasts and a light hand in the cellar, and his children run the estate today. Morgon, mor-GOHN, is one of the ten crus, the top villages of Beaujolais.

In the glass it is bright ruby. It tastes of crushed strawberry and cherry with a floral lift, silky in texture, with very low tannin and bright acidity.

That is why it is on the list for the Eggs Owen. Tannin and egg clash, and this wine has almost none, so the soft-boiled egg and the hollandaise stay sweet while the juicy fruit meets the red wine-braised short rib débris. It is a red that suits the morning.

value.a:
Jean Foillard's Morgon Côte du Py 2022 is the sweet spot bottle with the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits: bin 28362, $115.

Foillard, fwah-YAR, farms in Villié-Morgon and is one of the growers who led Beaujolais back to natural, whole-bunch Gamay with native yeasts. Morgon is one of the ten crus, and the Côte du Py, koht dew PEE, is the hill at its center, its best known slope.

In the glass it is deeper in color than most Beaujolais. It tastes of dark cherry and plum with a savory, stony edge, medium in body, with soft but present tannin and a long, fresh finish.

It is here as the step up from the Clos de la Roilette. Where the Fleurie is bright and light, the Côte du Py has the depth to meet smoky tasso and the fried pimento cheese grit cake, and its tannin still stays gentle enough for the Creole sauce and spice.

value.a:
Domaine Jean Grivot's Les Charmois Nuits-Saint-Georges 2013 is the sweet spot bottle with the Blackened Tofu: bin 23374, $138.

Grivot, gree-VOH, is a family domaine in Vosne-Romanée, run today by Mathilde Grivot. Les Charmois, lay shar-MWAH, is a village-level vineyard just south of the town of Nuits-Saint-Georges. The wine is Pinot Noir, aged in barrel, and it has had thirteen years in bottle.

That age is the point. In the glass it is a lighter, garnet-edged ruby. The fresh cherry of youth has turned to dried cherry, forest floor and mushroom, with silky tannin and fresh acidity still holding it up.

It is on the list for the tofu because mature Pinot Noir and mushrooms speak the same language: the savory notes echo the preserved shiitakes, the acidity lifts the rice grits, and the soft tannin stays calm under the blackened crust. It is also a fair price for red Burgundy with real age.

value.a:
Domaine Georges Roumier's Clos de la Bussière 2014, a Morey-Saint-Denis Premier Cru, is the celebration bottle with the Blackened Tofu: bin 287142, $320.

Roumier, roo-MYAY, is a family domaine in Chambolle-Musigny and one of the most sought-after growers in Burgundy; its Grand Crus are hard to find anywhere. The Clos de la Bussière, kloh duh lah bew-SYAIR, is a walled Premier Cru in neighboring Morey-Saint-Denis that Roumier owns alone, a monopole.

At twelve years it is a deep ruby turning garnet. It tastes of dark cherry and plum with earth, iron and spice, firm but silky tannin and real depth, a more rustic, earthy side of Roumier than its Chambolle wines.

It is here because it is the gentlest way into a legendary name, and because its earthy depth is made for umami: the preserved shiitakes and rice grits meet it head on, and the silk carries the blackened spice.

Marquis d'Angerville's Clos des Ducs Volnay Premier Cru 2014 is the celebration bottle with the Eggs Owen: bin 34351, $380.

D'Angerville, dahn-zhair-VEEL, is a family domaine in Volnay, farmed biodynamically, and one of the names that defines the village. The Clos des Ducs, kloh day DEWK, is the walled Premier Cru beside the house, and the domaine owns it alone, a monopole.

It is the top of the ladder for the Eggs Owen, after the Lapierre Morgon and the Tollot-Beaut Les Lavières. Its depth meets the red wine-braised short rib and the marchand de vin, and its silk stays gentle with the soft-boiled egg and hollandaise: a brunch bottle for a birthday or an anniversary.

value.a:
Domaine Jean Grivot's Echézeaux Grand Cru 2011 is the celebration bottle with the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast: bin 26764, $450.

Grivot, gree-VOH, is a family domaine in Vosne-Romanée, run by Mathilde Grivot, and one of the village's reference names. Echézeaux, eh-shay-ZOH, is a Grand Cru, Burgundy's top tier, on the slope beside Vosne-Romanée above the Clos de Vougeot.

At fifteen years it is a garnet-edged ruby. The fruit has moved past bright cherry into dark cherry, rose and spice with forest floor, and the tannin has turned silky; the finish is long and layered.

It is on the list as the grand step for duck: rich enough to meet the breast, with fruit for the cane syrup peaches and a nutty, savory side for the candied hazelnuts. Grand Cru Burgundy with real age is rare on any list, and at $450 it is the gentlest Grand Cru red we carry from a top Vosne name.

The Domaine de la Romanée-Conti Echézeaux Grand Cru 2015 is the gentlest priced red from the domaine on our list: bin 26733, $1650.

The Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, which guests often call DRC, is in Vosne-Romanée and is the most famous wine estate in the world. It owns the whole of two Grand Crus, Romanée-Conti and La Tâche, and parcels in others, Echézeaux, eh-shay-ZOH, among them. The domaine works with whole bunches, which gives its reds a spicy, lifted freshness.

At eleven years it is a bright, medium ruby. It tastes of red and black cherry, rose and spice, silky and lifted, the most open of the domaine's reds when young.

It is here because guests ask for DRC by name, and the Echézeaux is the way in. The list carries the domaine's Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Romanée-Saint-Vivant and others above it; this is the bottle for a guest who wants the name for a milestone.

value.a:
Domaine Armand Rousseau's Clos Saint-Jacques Gevrey-Chambertin Premier Cru 2019 is one of the famous bottles on our list: bin 23651, $2300.

Rousseau, roo-SOH, is the family domaine that made Gevrey-Chambertin's name, with holdings in Chambertin and other Grand Crus. The Clos Saint-Jacques, kloh san ZHAHK, is a walled Premier Cru on the slope above the village that many rank beside the Grand Crus, and the market prices it that way.

At seven years it is still young. In the glass it is a deep ruby, and it tastes of dark cherry, raspberry and spice, deep but refined, with fine tannin and great length.

It is on the list because collectors ask for Rousseau by name, and bottles are hard to find. It suits beef and game, the Chateaubriand or lamb, and it shows best decanted by the sommelier. For most guests the right move is to listen, confirm the bottle and bring the sommelier.

La Tâche, lah TAHSH, is a Grand Cru in Vosne-Romanée, beside the Romanée-Conti vineyard, and the domaine owns it entire, a monopole. The Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, guests' DRC, makes its reds with whole bunches, and La Tâche is often called the spicier, more exuberant sibling of Romanée-Conti.

At fourteen years it is a deep, glowing ruby. It tastes of black cherry, rose, exotic spice and a savory depth, silky and very long.

It is here because collectors come to Brennan's for bottles like this, and our list carries La Tâche in several vintages. It is the centerpiece of an evening rather than a match for one dish; duck, squab or the Chateaubriand will sit happily beside it. Your job is to recognize the request, confirm the bottle and bring the sommelier.

value.a:
Romanée-Conti Grand Cru 2014 from the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti is the most famous red wine in the world, and on our list: bin 28538, $12500.

The vineyard, roh-mah-NAY kohn-TEE, lies in Vosne-Romanée and covers under two hectares. The domaine owns all of it and takes its name from it; the other monopole, La Tâche, lies beside it. So little is made each year that a bottle is rare anywhere, and the domaine sells it in very small allocations.

At twelve years it is a medium, glowing ruby. It tastes of red and black fruit, rose, spice and earth, weightless and silky, with a finish that goes on and on: the benchmark every Pinot Noir is measured against.

It is on the list because Brennan's keeps a cellar that collectors travel for, and the list carries Romanée-Conti in several vintages. It is an evening in itself. If a guest asks, take it seriously, confirm the bottle with the sommelier and let the sommelier lead.

value.a:
Les Cadrans de Lassègue 2021, a Saint-Émilion Grand Cru, is the gentlest priced anchor on our Bordeaux pages: bin 28352, $60.

It is the second wine of Château Lassègue, lah-SEG, in Saint-Émilion, owned by Jackson Family Wines. A second wine is made from the younger vines and the parcels that do not go into the main wine; the name Cadrans, kah-DRAHN, comes from the sundials on the château's front. It is mostly Merlot with Cabernet Franc, aged a few months in part new oak.

Right Bank Bordeaux is softer than the Médoc. In the glass it is a bright purple-ruby, and it tastes of red cherry, plum and a little spice, with soft, refined tannin and a fresh finish.

It is on the list for the guest who wants claret without weight or a big price: with roast chicken, pork, a lunch steak or a burger at the bar. It drinks well now, at five years.

La Chapelle de Meyney 2018, from Saint-Estèphe, is the value bottle with the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak and an anchor of our Bordeaux: bin 26311, $80.

A second wine comes from the younger vines and the parcels that do not go into the main wine. This one is mostly Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and a little Petit Verdot, aged in oak; the exact mix in 2018 is a question for the sommelier.

value.a:
Château Haut-Bages Libéral 2018, a fifth growth Pauillac, is an anchor of our Bordeaux at the start of the sweet spot: bin 26723, $135.

Haut-Bages Libéral, oh BAHZH lee-bay-RAL, is one of the fifth growths in the 1855 classification of the Médoc. Its largest parcel lies beside Château Latour, and the estate, run by Claire Villars-Lurton, is certified organic and biodynamic. It is mostly Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, aged in French oak with part new barrels.

Pauillac, poy-YAK, is the home of three of the five first growths and of firm, cedary Cabernet. At eight years this is a deep ruby, and it tastes of blackcurrant, graphite and cedar, with ripe fruit and firm, polished tannin.

It is on the list as the fair-priced way into classed growth Pauillac. It suits beef and lamb, the Chateaubriand above all, and it opens with an hour in a decanter.

Château Bellegrave 2019, a Pomerol, is an anchor of our Bordeaux in the sweet spot: bin 26111, $190.

Pomerol, pom-uh-ROLL, is a small village on the Right Bank of Bordeaux, beside Saint-Émilion, known for plush, generous Merlot and never classified. Bellegrave, bel-GRAHV, is a family estate in the southwest of the village, owned by the Bouldy family since 1951 and farmed organically on clay and gravel. It is mostly Merlot with Cabernet Franc.

It is here as an honest Pomerol at a fair price, for the guest who finds Cabernet too firm. It suits duck, roast pork and beef in gentler sauces, and it lets a guest taste Pomerol without reaching for the grand names on the same page.

value.a:
Château Talbot 2019, a Saint-Julien fourth growth, is the sweet spot bottle with the Roasted Chateaubriand: bin 33111, $245.

Talbot, tal-BOH, is a fourth growth in the 1855 classification of the Médoc. Saint-Julien, san zhoo-LYAN, is the village between Pauillac and Margaux, known for balanced, elegant Cabernet. The wine is mostly Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, aged in French oak.

At seven years it is a deep ruby. It tastes of blackcurrant and plum with cedar and cigar box, medium to full in body, with firm but fine tannin and a long, savory finish.

It is on the list for the Chateaubriand because a French beef course wants French structure: the tannin meets the tenderloin, and the cedar and fruit stand up to the rich sauce Foyot. It is the classic Bordeaux bottle for a dish for two, a step above the Haut-Bages Libéral and below the Pichon Lalande.

Grand-Puy-Lacoste, grahn PWEE lah-KOST, is one of the fifth growths of the 1855 classification, owned by the Borie family and often called one of the best values in the Médoc for classic, long-lived Pauillac. It is led by Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot.

At eighteen years it is a deep garnet. The young blackcurrant has turned to cassis and cedar, with tobacco, earth and graphite, and the firm Pauillac tannin has resolved into a long, savory finish.

It is here because steak, béarnaise and a sunny side up egg want structure, and mature Bordeaux gives structure without harshness. It is the top of the ladder for the hanger steak, after La Chapelle de Meyney, and the list carries it in six vintages, so the 2008 is the one to name.

value.a:
Château Pichon-Longueville Comtesse de Lalande 2004, a second growth Pauillac, is the celebration bottle with the Roasted Chateaubriand: bin 26411, $325.

Pichon Lalande, as most people call it, pee-SHOHN lah-LAHND, is a second growth in the 1855 classification. It sits across the road from Château Latour and has been owned since 2007 by the Champagne house Louis Roederer. It is led by Cabernet Sauvignon but carries more Merlot than its neighbors, which gives it a silky elegance among the wines of Pauillac.

At twenty-two years it is a garnet-edged ruby. It tastes of cassis, cedar, tobacco and dried rose, with silky, resolved tannin and a long, elegant finish.

It is on the list for the Chateaubriand because tenderloin is lean and tender, and wants a wine with depth but no hard edges. The silk meets the beef, and the depth stands up to the rich sauce Foyot. It is mature classed growth Bordeaux at a fair price for its rank.

value.a:
Clos L'Église 2019, a Pomerol, is an anchor of our Bordeaux above the sweet spot: bin 25623, $325.

Clos L'Église, kloh lay-GLEEZ, is a small estate in the heart of Pomerol, the Right Bank village of plush, generous Merlot. Sylviane Garcin-Cathiard bought it in 1997, and her family run it; the vines are farmed organically, and the wine is aged in new French oak. It is Merlot with Cabernet Franc.

At seven years it is a deep, inky ruby. It tastes of black cherry, plum and mocha with violet and spice, rich, polished and long, still young.

It is on the list as the step between the Bellegrave and the grand names of Pomerol on the same page: a serious bottle that gives a guest the Pomerol richness at a third of the price of the famous names. It suits duck, lamb and the Chateaubriand, and it wants an hour in a decanter.

value.a:
Château Haut-Brion 2002 is the gentlest priced first growth on our list: bin 26732, $700.

Haut-Brion, oh bree-OHN, is one of the five first growths of Bordeaux and the only one of the 1855 classification outside the Médoc. It lies in Pessac on the edge of the city of Bordeaux, in what is now the Pessac-Léognan appellation of the Graves. The blend is Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon with some Cabernet Franc, and its gravel soils give a smoky, earthy character the Médoc first growths do not share.

At twenty-four years it is a mature garnet. It tastes of cassis and plum with tobacco, smoke and gravel, silky and resolved, with a long, savory finish.

It is here because guests come to Brennan's for the first growths, and this is the way in: a famous name with real age at the friendliest price of the five. It suits the Chateaubriand or lamb, and the sommelier decants it.

value.a:
Château Mouton-Rothschild 2005 is one of the famous first growths on our list: bin 27232, $1400.

Mouton, moo-TOHN, is in Pauillac and was promoted from second to first growth in 1973, the only change ever made to the 1855 classification. Since the 1940s every vintage has carried a label by a different artist, which makes every bottle a talking point; which artist made the 2005 label is a question for the sommelier. The wine is led by Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and Cabernet Franc.

At twenty-one years it is a deep garnet-ruby. It tastes of cassis, blackberry, cedar and coffee, with Mouton's famous opulence, the firm tannin softening and a very long finish.

It is here because guests ask for the first growths by name, and Mouton is the one with a story to tell. It suits the Chateaubriand, lamb or prime beef, and it wants a long decant from the sommelier.

value.a:
Château Margaux 2007 is the gentlest priced vintage of Château Margaux on our list: bin 34334, $1425.

Château Margaux, shah-TOH mar-GOH, is one of the five first growths of 1855, and the one that shares its name with its village, Margaux, in the southern Médoc. Margaux is known for the most perfumed, silky Cabernet in Bordeaux, and the château is its benchmark. The wine is led by Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.

At nineteen years it is a deep garnet. It tastes of cassis, violet and rose with cedar and spice, silky, fine tannin and great perfume, more grace than power.

It is here because guests ask for Château Margaux by name, often for a birthday or an anniversary, and our list carries it in many vintages. It suits lamb, the Chateaubriand and roast veal, and the sommelier decants it.

value.a:
Château Cheval Blanc 2008 is the Right Bank legend on our list: bin 288242, $1450.

Cheval Blanc, shuh-VAL BLAHN, is the most famous estate in Saint-Émilion, right on the border with Pomerol. It was ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A, the top rank of Saint-Émilion, when this vintage was made, as the list prints. It is unusual in Bordeaux for leading with Cabernet Franc, with Merlot, which gives it perfume and freshness.

At eighteen years it is a mature ruby with garnet at the rim. It tastes of red and black fruit, violet, mint and spice, silky, fresh and very long.

It is here because collectors ask for it as they ask for the first growths, and it is the Right Bank's answer to them. It suits duck, lamb and veal, and a guest who prefers silk to power. The list carries it in many vintages, so the 2008 is the one to name.

value.a:
Château Lafite-Rothschild 2004 is one of the famous first growths on our list: bin 22274, $2100.

Lafite, lah-FEET, is perhaps the most famous name in Bordeaux. It was listed first among the first growths in the 1855 classification, it lies in the north of Pauillac by Saint-Estèphe, and it is owned by the Rothschild family. It is led by Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot.

Of the three Pauillac first growths, Lafite is the elegant one: Latour is power, Mouton opulence. At twenty-two years this is a garnet-edged ruby, and it tastes of cassis, cedar, graphite and pencil shavings, with fine, refined tannin and a long finish.

It is here because the name sells itself, and guests ask for it for the biggest occasions. The list carries Lafite in many vintages, so name the 2004. It suits lamb or the Chateaubriand, and the sommelier decants it.

value.a:
Château Latour 2005 is one of the famous first growths on our list: bin 261510, $2130.

Latour, lah-TOOR, is one of the five first growths of 1855. It lies in the south of Pauillac, by the Gironde estuary and beside Pichon Lalande, named for the old tower that still stands in its vineyard. It is led by Cabernet Sauvignon, and it is known as the most powerful and long-lived of the first growths.

At twenty-one years this is still young for its kind. It is a deep, dark ruby, and it tastes of blackcurrant, cassis, cedar and walnut, with great depth and firm tannin.

It is here because guests ask for the first growths, and Latour is the one for a guest who wants power. It wants the Chateaubriand or prime beef and a long decant. Our list also carries a Latour 1946 at $4100 among the Selections from our Birth Year, the year Brennan's opened.

value.a:
Pétrus 1980 is a mature Pétrus on our list: bin 21131, $7700.

Pétrus, pay-TROOS, is the most famous Merlot in the world. It comes from a small plateau of clay in Pomerol, on the Right Bank, almost entirely Merlot and made in tiny quantities. Pomerol has never had a classification, so Pétrus carries no rank: its name is enough.

At forty-six years this bottle has moved far from fruit. It is a brick-edged garnet, and it should taste of dried plum and fig, truffle, leather and earth, soft and velvety. At this age every bottle is its own, shaped by the cork and the cellar, so the sommelier opens it with care and tastes it before it is poured.

It is here for the collector who wants a mature Pétrus, a rare thing anywhere. Keep the food simple, roast squab or duck, and let the bottle be the event. The list also prints a Pétrus 1989 at $14000; La Fleur-Pétrus, a different Pomerol, appears in younger vintages.

Crozes-Hermitage, krohz air-mee-TAHZH, is the larger appellation in the hills around the great hill of Hermitage in the Northern Rhône, where Syrah is the red grape.

La Louisianne comes from old vines on the middle terraces, mostly Grenache with Mourvèdre and a little Cinsault and Syrah, co-fermented in concrete and aged in oak. It is a young, deep ruby. It tastes of ripe red and black cherry with garrigue herbs and spice, generous in body, with soft tannin.

It is here for the filet because ripe Grenache fruit meets beef and garlic spinach without the weight of a big red at breakfast, and because a Louisiana name on a Gigondas makes guests smile.

André Perret's Condrieu 2019 is the one white on our Rhône cards and an anchor of the page: bin 22331, $165.

Condrieu, kohn-dree-UH, is a tiny appellation on steep granite slopes in the Northern Rhône and the home of the Viognier grape. André Perret farms in Chavanay, at its southern end, where his family grew orchards; he took over from his father in the early 1980s and is counted among the masters of Viognier. The list prints only Condrieu, so whether this is his classic bottling or the Coteau de Chéry is a question for the sommelier.

It is a dry white, a deep gold at seven years. It tastes of apricot, peach and honeysuckle, with a rich, rounded texture and a fresh, mineral finish.

It is here for the guest who wants a rich white that is not Chardonnay. Its perfume and texture love butter and rich seafood: the Louisiana BBQ Lobster, the Pecan Gulf Fish and crab.

value.a:
René Rostaing's Côte-Rôtie Ampodium 2012 is an anchor of our Rhône in the sweet spot: bin 24753, $170.

Côte-Rôtie, koht roh-TEE, means the roasted slope: steep terraces above the Rhône at Ampuis, at the northern end of the valley, and the most perfumed Syrah in France. Rostaing, roh-STAN, is a grower in Ampuis, and Ampodium, once called Classique, blends his many parcels across the appellation, made with whole bunches and aged in large, mostly old casks.

At fourteen years it is a garnet-edged ruby. It tastes of blackberry, violet, black olive, smoked meat and pepper, silky and fragrant, with a long, savory finish.

It is here because Côte-Rôtie with real age is a rare thing at this price, and the perfumed side of Syrah wins over Pinot Noir lovers. It suits lamb, duck and beef with herbs. The list carries Rostaing's single-vineyard wines too, at higher prices.

Domaine du Pegau's Cuvée Réservée Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2020 is the sweet spot bottle with the Petite Filet Mignon: bin 24751, $195.

Pegau, peh-GOH, is the Féraud family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, and the Cuvée Réservée is its flagship, made the traditional way: mostly Grenache with Syrah, Mourvèdre and a share of the other permitted varieties, fermented with whole bunches in cement and aged two years in large old casks. Châteauneuf-du-Pape, shah-toh-NUF dew PAHP, is the great name of the Southern Rhône.

At six years it is a deep ruby. It tastes of kirsch and plum with garrigue herbs, leather and spice, generous, warm and long.

It is here for the filet because the body meets beef and the garlic spinach, and the spice flatters the crisp potato rösti. It is a step up from the Saint Damien Gigondas and a classic, old-school Châteauneuf for a guest who knows the name.

value.a:
Château de Beaucastel's Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2007, an Oenothèque release, is the celebration bottle with the Petite Filet Mignon: bin 25252, $275.

Beaucastel, boh-kah-STEL, is the Perrin family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, famous for using every permitted variety and for a high share of Mourvèdre, which gives savory, long-lived wines. Oenothèque, ay-noh-TEK, means a wine library: the family keep bottles of each vintage in their own cellar and release some years later, labeled with the date they left the cellar, so the storage is beyond question.

At nineteen years it is a mature garnet. It tastes of dried cherry, leather, truffle and garrigue, with silky tannin and savory depth.

It is here because tender beef wants a red with softened tannin, and age gives exactly that. It is the top of the ladder for the filet, after the Saint Damien and the Pegau, and a mature Châteauneuf with certain provenance is a rare find on any list.

value.a:
Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe's La Crau Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2014 is the celebration bottle with the Creole Hanger Steak: bin 284217, $295.

Vieux Télégraphe, vyuh tay-lay-GRAHF, is the Brunier family's estate on the high La Crau plateau of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, named for the old signal telegraph tower that once stood there. The vines grow among large, round stones that hold the day's heat. La Crau is the estate's main red, mostly Grenache with Mourvèdre and Syrah.

At twelve years it is a garnet-edged ruby. It tastes of kirsch and dried cherry with garrigue herbs, pepper and leather, warm, savory and silky.

It is here for the hanger steak because Creole spice and chili crisp punish hard tannin, and an older Châteauneuf has warmth, ripe fruit and soft tannin instead. The garrigue meets the pepita persillade, and the depth stands up to the beef.

value.a:
Auguste Clape's Cornas 2016 is an anchor of our Rhône: bin 34534, $318.

Cornas, kor-NAHS, is a small, steep granite amphitheater at the south of the Northern Rhône, and its red is all Syrah. The Clape family, KLAHP, is the name that defines it: they make wine the traditional way, with whole bunches and old casks, and their Cornas is the benchmark other growers are measured against.

At ten years it is a deep, dark ruby. It tastes of blackberry and black cherry, violet, pepper, smoke and earth, with firm tannin that is starting to open and a long, pure finish.

It is here for the guest who loves Syrah and wants the real thing: rugged, pure and savory, not polished. It suits lamb, venison and a peppery steak, and it wants an hour in a decanter. The list carries Clape in several vintages, so name the 2016.

value.a:
Domaine Jean-Louis Chave's Hermitage 2013 is one of the famous bottles on our Rhône pages: bin 24442, $490.

Hermitage, air-mee-TAHZH, is a single granite hill above the Rhône at Tain, and its Syrah is among the most long-lived red wines in France. The Chave family, SHAHV, from Mauves across the river, is the grower most associated with the hill. Their Hermitage is blended from several plots, each with its own soil and character, which is what gives it its completeness.

At thirteen years it is a deep, dark ruby. It tastes of blackberry, cassis, violet, smoke and iron, deep and firm, with a very long finish, still young for its kind.

value.a:
Château Rayas Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2011 is the cult bottle on our Rhône pages: bin 22458, $1200.

Rayas, rah-YAHS, is the Reynaud family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Its parcels are sandy and set among woods, cooler than most of the appellation, and its Châteauneuf is made from Grenache alone, in an old-fashioned cellar that rarely receives visitors. Where most Châteauneuf blends many varieties and leans dark and warm, Rayas is pale and fine.

At fifteen years it is a translucent, garnet-edged red. It tastes of strawberry, raspberry and kirsch, rose, spice and earth, silky and perfumed, closer to a great Burgundy in feel than to its neighbors.

It is here because collectors ask for Rayas by name, and bottles are scarce. It suits duck, squab and lamb, and it often shows best poured straight, as the sommelier decides. The list carries Rayas in three vintages, so name the 2011.

value.a:
Château Latour 1946 is the grandest of our four Birth Year bottles, wines from 1946, the year Brennan’s opened: bin 27340, $4100.

Latour is in Pauillac, on the Left Bank of Bordeaux, its vineyard running down toward the Gironde estuary around an old tower, the l’Enclos. In the classification of 1855 it was ranked one of the first growths, the top rank of the Médoc, and today it is owned by François Pinault. The wine is Cabernet Sauvignon led, with Merlot, aged in oak.

At eighty years, what is in the glass is history more than fruit. Expect a pale, bricked color and a soft, fragile frame: cedar, dried fruit, leather and earth. No two bottles this old are the same, because each has lived in its own cellar under its own cork.

It is on the list for the guest marking a milestone born in 1946, or a table that wants to drink something as old as the restaurant itself.

Château Trotanoy 1946 is the Pomerol among our four Birth Year bottles, from the year Brennan’s opened: bin 27345, $3700.

Trotanoy, troh-tah-NWAH, is a small estate in Pomerol, on the Right Bank of Bordeaux near Libourne. It belongs to the Moueix family, the merchants whose name also stands behind Dominus in Napa. Pomerol has no official classification, yet its best estates are among the most sought after in Bordeaux. The wine is mostly Merlot, with Cabernet Franc.

Merlot gives a rounder, softer wine than the Cabernet of the Médoc, and at eighty years that softness has become something delicate. Expect a garnet color browning at the rim, and dried plum, truffle, earth and a faded sweetness. Each bottle has aged in its own way, so the sommelier judges it at the table.

It is here for the guest born in 1946, or the table celebrating with a wine as old as Brennan’s, who prefers the gentler Right Bank style.

value.a:
Château-Figeac 1946 is one of our four Birth Year bottles, wines from the year Brennan’s opened: bin 27362, $3200.

Figeac, fee-ZHAK, lies in Saint-Émilion on the Right Bank of Bordeaux, on gravel soils beside Cheval Blanc near the Pomerol border. Most of Saint-Émilion is Merlot country, but Figeac has long grown Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc in a large share, which gives it a fresher, more cedary style than its neighbors. The Manoncourt family ran it for decades, and in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification it was raised to the top rank, Premier Grand Cru Classé A.

In the glass at eighty years: a bricked, delicate wine of dried red fruit, tobacco leaf, cedar and earth, the Cabernet still giving it a thread of freshness. Every bottle has aged on its own path.

It is on the list for a 1946 celebration, and for the guest who loves the Right Bank but likes a firmer line.

value.a:
López de Heredia’s Viña Cubillo Crianza 2016 is a first pick for the Roost Burger and the Spanish anchor under $100: bin 1379, $70.

R. López de Heredia is one of the oldest bodegas in Haro, the wine town of Rioja Alta, and still family run. They work the old way: grapes picked by hand, fermented in old wooden vats, then aged about three years in old American oak barrels from their own cooperage, and longer in bottle before release. Viña Cubillo is their youngest red, mostly Tempranillo with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo.

In the glass it is a light garnet. It tastes of dried cherry, strawberry, leather and gentle spice, light in tannin, with lively acidity.

It is on the list because it gives real age and character for very little: a Crianza that drinks like a much older wine. With the burger, its soft tannin and savory fruit meet short rib, bacon and cheese.

Answer: A Rioja aged in oak and bottle before release. López de Heredia ages theirs far longer than the rule asks, about three years in barrel.

value.a:
Fèlsina Chianti Classico 2022 is our anchor for Italian red under $100: bin 14062, $90.

Fattoria di Fèlsina, FEL-see-nah, farms vineyards at Castelnuovo Berardenga, on the warm southern edge of the Chianti Classico zone, northeast of Siena. Chianti Classico is the historic heart of Chianti, between Florence and Siena, and Sangiovese is its grape. Fèlsina’s Chianti Classico is all Sangiovese, fermented in steel and aged about a year in medium-size Slavonian oak casks, so the fruit leads.

At four years it is a bright ruby. It tastes of sour cherry, violet and dried herbs with a touch of earth, with firm acidity and fine, dusty tannin.

It is on the list because it is the easiest Italian bottle to put on any table. The acidity loves tomato, mushrooms, roast chicken and pork, and the price is gentle. For a deeper, single vineyard Fèlsina, the Rancia Riserva is the next step.

value.a:
The Produttori del Barbaresco Barbaresco 2020 is our anchor for Nebbiolo under $100: bin 16122, $95.

Barbaresco is a small village in the Langhe hills of Piedmont, in northwest Italy, and its wine is made from Nebbiolo. The Produttori del Barbaresco is the village cooperative: some fifty grower families who bring their grapes to one cellar. This classic Barbaresco is blended from many of their vineyards and aged in large oak casks. In the best years they also bottle single vineyard wines, such as the Asili.

Nebbiolo is pale in the glass and firm on the tongue. Expect red cherry, rose, dried herbs and tar, with high acidity and grippy tannin.

It is on the list because it is the benchmark: true Barbaresco from the people who farm it, at a price that lets a guest try Nebbiolo with dinner. With beef, mushrooms or a butter sauce, the tannin softens and the perfume rises.

CVNE Imperial Reserva 2018 is our Spanish anchor just over $100, between the Cubillo and the 904: bin 10422, $110.

CVNE, said KOO-nay, stands for Compañía Vinícola del Norte de España, a historic house in the railway station quarter of Haro, the wine town of Rioja Alta. Its Imperial label is kept for Reserva and Gran Reserva. A Reserva is aged in oak barrels and then in bottle before release, so it arrives ready to drink. This one is mostly Tempranillo, with a little Graciano and Mazuelo; the exact mix in 2018 is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is deep ruby with a touch of brick. It tastes of red and black cherry, plum, sweet spice and leather, medium to full in body, with polished tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list as classic Rioja at its most polished: a little richer than the Cubillo and much gentler in price than the 904.

value.a:
Fèlsina Rancia Chianti Classico Riserva 2019 is an Italian anchor in the sweet spot: bin 16433, $165.

Rancia, RAHN-chah, is the most famous vineyard of Fattoria di Fèlsina, at Castelnuovo Berardenga in the warm southern corner of Chianti Classico, near Siena. Fèlsina bottles it on its own as a Riserva, which means longer aging before release. It is all Sangiovese, aged in oak barrels and then in bottle.

At seven years it is a deep ruby beginning to show garnet. It tastes of dark cherry and plum with dried herbs, leather and spice, firm but fine in tannin, with the long, savory acidity Sangiovese is loved for.

It is on the list as the serious face of Chianti Classico, a single vineyard wine that ages for decades, and the natural step up from Fèlsina’s Chianti Classico at $90. With roast lamb, wild mushrooms or the Chateaubriand, it opens beautifully.

value.a:
The Produttori del Barbaresco Asili 2019 is our Piedmont anchor in the sweet spot: bin 21742, $185.

Asili, AH-zee-lee, is one of the most celebrated vineyards in the village of Barbaresco, in the Langhe hills of Piedmont. The Produttori del Barbaresco, the village cooperative of some fifty grower families, bottles its members’ best single vineyards on their own only in the great years, usually as Riservas, and aged in large oak casks. Asili is often the most perfumed of them.

In the glass it is a pale, bright garnet. It smells of rose petal and red cherry and tastes of cherry, orange peel and spice, with silky but firm tannin and lifting acidity that carries a long finish.

It is on the list because it is great cru Barbaresco at a fair price, and the natural step up from the Produttori’s classic Barbaresco at $95. With the Chateaubriand, mushrooms or truffle, it sings.

value.a:
Il Poggione Brunello di Montalcino 2018 is an Italian anchor in the sweet spot: bin 17832, $198.

Brunello di Montalcino is Sangiovese from the hill town of Montalcino in southern Tuscany, one of Italy’s great reds. The rules ask for long aging, years in barrel and bottle, before release. Il Poggione, eel poh-JOH-neh, is the Franceschi family’s estate at Sant’Angelo in Colle, in the warm south of the zone, and a historic name in Brunello. It ages the wine in large oak casks in the traditional way.

At eight years it is a deep garnet. It tastes of dark cherry and plum with dried herbs, leather and a little balsamic warmth, with firm tannin and bright acidity that keep it fresh.

It is on the list as the classic Brunello: generous, traditional and fairly priced. With the Chateaubriand, roast lamb or an aged cheese, the tannin softens and the fruit comes forward.

value.a:
Flor de Pingus 2022 is our Spanish anchor in the sweet spot, from one of Spain’s cult estates: bin 16161, $215.

Dominio de Pingus was created by the Danish winemaker Peter Sisseck at La Horra, in Ribera del Duero, on the high plateau of Castilla y León, north of Madrid. Its top wine, Pingus, is made in tiny amounts; Flor de Pingus is the estate’s second wine, from younger and other vineyards, with the same care. The grape is Tinto Fino, the local name for Tempranillo, farmed biodynamically and aged in French oak.

At four years it is a deep, inky purple. It tastes of blackberry, black cherry, licorice and graphite, with ripe, dense tannin and a fresh line from the altitude.

It is on the list for the guest who wants Spanish power rather than Rioja’s mellow age, and for big meat: the Chateaubriand, grilled steak or lamb.

value.a:
La Rioja Alta Gran Reserva 904 2015 is the sweet spot bottle with the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak at lunch and an anchor of our Spanish reds: bin 179221, $250.

La Rioja Alta is a historic house in the railway station quarter of Haro, the wine town of Rioja Alta, and one of the keepers of traditional Rioja. A Gran Reserva is the longest aged level: the 904 is Tempranillo with a little Graciano, aged about four years in American oak barrels made in the house’s own cooperage, then years more in bottle before release.

In the glass it is a garnet turning brick at the rim. It tastes of dried cherry, strawberry, tobacco, vanilla, leather and sweet spice, silky in texture with mellow tannin and a long, savory finish.

It is on the list as grand Rioja at its most classic. With the hanger steak, its gentle tannin and spice meet the Creole seasoning, smoked potato pavé and béarnaise.

value.a:
Bartolo Mascarello Barolo 2017 is our Piedmont anchor in the celebration tier: bin 184221, $340.

Barolo is Nebbiolo from a handful of villages in the Langhe hills of Piedmont, and Bartolo Mascarello is one of its most revered names: a small family cellar in the village of Barolo, now run by Maria Teresa Mascarello. They are traditionalists. Where most estates bottle single vineyards, they blend Nebbiolo from four vineyards in Barolo and La Morra, which is why the list prints La Morra beside the name. The wine ferments with long skin contact and ages in large old oak casks, never new barrels.

In the glass it is pale garnet. It tastes of sour cherry, rose, tar, licorice and dried herbs, with high acidity and firm, fine tannin and a long finish.

It is on the list for the Barolo lover, and with nine vintages printed, for the guest who wants to choose a year.

Gaja, GUY-ah, is the family winery in the village of Barbaresco, in the Langhe hills of Piedmont. Angelo Gaja made it one of the most famous names in Italian wine, and his family runs it today. This is their flagship Barbaresco, all Nebbiolo from the family’s own vineyards in the village, made in a polished, precise style. The list prints it simply as Gaja, on the Barbaresco page.

At fourteen years it is a garnet with an orange rim. It tastes of red cherry, rose, dried orange peel, tobacco and spice, with refined tannin and fresh acidity that carry a long finish.

It is on the list for the guest who knows the name and the guest who wants a great Italian bottle with age already on it. With the Chateaubriand or anything earthy and buttery, it is at its best.

value.a:
Biondi Santi Brunello di Montalcino 2012 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 18542, $425.

Biondi Santi, bee-OHN-dee SAHN-tee, is the family credited with creating Brunello di Montalcino in the nineteenth century, at their estate Tenuta Greppo outside the Tuscan hill town of Montalcino. Since 2016 the estate has been owned by the EPI group of the Descours family, the same owners as Piper-Heidsieck and Rare, both poured here. The annata is the regular Brunello, as opposed to the Riserva: all Sangiovese, aged years in large Slavonian oak casks before release.

At fourteen years it is a garnet with an orange rim. It is elegant rather than powerful: sour cherry, dried rose, leather, tobacco and earth, with high acidity and fine, firm tannin.

value.a:
Sassicaia 2018 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 32686, $515.

Sassicaia, sahs-see-KAI-ah, is made at Tenuta San Guido, the Incisa della Rocchetta family estate at Bolgheri on the Tuscan coast. The family planted Cabernet on stony ground there when Italian law and opinion said great wine came only from native grapes, and Sassicaia became the first of the Super Tuscans. It is now the only Italian estate with an appellation of its own, Bolgheri Sassicaia. The wine is Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc, aged in French oak barrels.

At eight years it is deep ruby. It is elegant rather than heavy: blackcurrant, cedar, graphite, Mediterranean herbs and violet, with fine, firm tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list for the guest who knows the legend and for a celebration with the Chateaubriand or lamb. The same estate’s Guidalberto is the gentler priced way into the style.

value.a:
Masseto 2011 is a famous name in our celebration tier, Italy’s most famous Merlot: bin 27143, $1080.

Masseto, mahs-SEH-toh, comes from a single hill of blue clay at Bolgheri, on the Tuscan coast. It was first bottled by Tenuta dell’Ornellaia, which is why the list prints it under that name, and it is now run as an estate of its own by the Frescobaldi family. The clay holds water and keeps the vines cool, which gives Merlot a depth it rarely finds. The wine is aged in new French oak.

At fifteen years it is deep garnet. It is opulent: plum, black cherry, chocolate, truffle and spice, with velvet tannin and a fresh, long finish.

It is on the list for the collector and for the grand celebration. With the Chateaubriand and its sauce Foyot, truffle or mushrooms, its richness meets its match.

value.a:
Chappellet Mountain Cuvée 2024 is our Napa anchor under $100: bin 14342, $90, printed in the Selections Under $100.

Chappellet, shap-uh-LAY, was founded by Donn and Molly Chappellet on Pritchard Hill, on the eastern hills of the Napa Valley, in 1967, and the family still runs it. Their top wines come from the steep, rocky estate. Mountain Cuvée is the friendlier blend: led by Cabernet Sauvignon, with Merlot and smaller amounts of the other Bordeaux grapes, from the estate and other Napa vineyards. The mix changes every year, and the 2024 blend is a question for the sommelier.

It is deep purple and young. It tastes of ripe black cherry, cassis, mocha and a little spice, with soft, supple tannin, so it drinks well now.

It is on the list as the easiest way into Napa red: a family name with real pedigree at a price that suits a burger at the Roost or a weekday steak.

value.a:
Frog’s Leap Estate Rutherford Cabernet Sauvignon 2021 is a Napa anchor in the sweet spot: bin 109222, $165.

Frog’s Leap is John Williams’s winery in Rutherford, in the middle of the Napa Valley. It is known for two things: farming organically, and dry farming, which means the vines get no irrigation and send their roots deep for water. The result is wine that tastes fresher and less heavy than much of Napa. The Estate Cabernet comes from Frog’s Leap’s own Rutherford vineyards.

At five years it is a bright, deep ruby. It tastes of red and black currant and cherry, with the dusty earth Rutherford is known for and a note of dried herbs, fresh acidity and fine, firm tannin.

It is on the list for the guest who finds big Napa too much, and for food: lamb, mushrooms, steak and the Chateaubriand. Older vintages, including a 1991, are on the list too.

value.a:
Caymus Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon 2023 is a first pick for the Roost Burger, and the Napa name many guests ask for: bin 1726, $180.

Caymus, KAY-mus, is the Wagner family’s winery in Rutherford, in the middle of the Napa Valley, run by Chuck Wagner and his family. It is known for a ripe, plush style of Cabernet Sauvignon: the grapes are picked ripe and the wine is aged in oak and made to be soft and generous young. The family also makes the Special Selection, our celebration Caymus.

At three years it is deep purple, almost opaque. It tastes of black cherry, cassis, cocoa, vanilla and sweet spice, full bodied, with soft, velvety tannin.

It is on the list because guests love it and ask for it. With the burger, its ripe fruit meets the tomato jam and the sweetness of the short rib, and its body handles the bacon, cheese and special sauce.

Shafer One Point Five 2023 is our Napa anchor at the top of the sweet spot: bin 183221, $250.

Shafer Vineyards, SHAY-fer, is a family estate in the Stags Leap District, a small appellation on the east side of the Napa Valley, below the rocky palisades. Stags Leap is known for Cabernet that is rich but velvety, with soft tannin. One Point Five is named for John Shafer, who founded the winery, and his son Doug, the generation and a half who made its name. At three years it is deep purple. It tastes of black cherry, blackberry, dark chocolate and violet, rich in body with fine, soft tannin.

It is on the list as the Stags Leap anchor, a step below Shafer’s famous Hillside Select in price, for a celebration steak or lamb.

value.a:
Inglenook Rubicon 2010, sold as a whole bottle, is a Napa anchor in the celebration tier: bin 18231, $360. It is the same wine we pour by the glass at $70.

Inglenook is one of the historic estates of Rutherford, in the middle of the Napa Valley, restored under Francis Ford Coppola’s family. Rubicon is its flagship, a Cabernet Sauvignon based blend. Our wine is the 2010, sixteen years old, a Napa legend with real age on it.

In the glass it is deep garnet. Age has softened the tannins, so it is powerful but silky: blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and earth.

It is on the list as a bottle for the table that has tasted the glass and wants more, and for a couple sharing the Roasted Chateaubriand with its sauce Foyot. At $70 a glass, a table having five glasses or more is better served by the bottle, which is when to mention it. Older Rubicon vintages, 2005 and 2009, are printed too.

value.a:
Silver Oak Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon 2020 is a first pick for the Roost Burger: bin 1588, $360.

Silver Oak Cellars was founded by Justin Meyer and Ray Duncan and is run by the Duncan family. It makes only Cabernet Sauvignon, in two bottlings, Napa Valley and Alexander Valley, and its signature is American oak: the wine is aged only in American oak barrels and then rested in bottle before release. American oak gives vanilla, dill and sweet spice in a way French oak does not, and guests often recognize it.

At six years it is deep ruby. It tastes of blackberry and black cherry with vanilla, dill and sweet spice, full bodied, smooth, with polished tannin.

It is on the list because it is a name people love to toast with. With the burger’s double short rib patties, bacon and cheese, it has the weight and ripeness to match; with a steak it is just as happy.

value.a:
Ridge Monte Bello 2012 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 16131, $410.

Ridge Vineyards makes Monte Bello from its vineyard high on a limestone ridge in the Santa Cruz Mountains, south of San Francisco, a world away from Napa. Paul Draper, its longtime winemaker, made it one of America’s great wines. It is a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with Merlot and a little Petit Verdot and Cabernet Franc, aged in American oak; the exact mix changes by year. Monte Bello stood beside the great Bordeaux at the Judgment of Paris tasting in 1976 and won the rematch thirty years later.

At fourteen years it is deep garnet. It is savory and fresh: blackcurrant, cedar, graphite, mint and earth, with fine, firm tannin and bright acidity.

It is on the list for the guest who knows the story and the one who loves Bordeaux and wants America’s answer, with lamb or the Chateaubriand.

value.a:
Joseph Phelps Insignia 2013 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 18727, $440.

Joseph Phelps Vineyards is in St. Helena, in the Napa Valley, and Insignia is its flagship. First made in 1974, it was California’s first proprietary Bordeaux-style blend: a wine named for itself rather than for a grape, chosen each year from the estate’s best lots. It is led by Cabernet Sauvignon with the other Bordeaux grapes and aged in new French oak; the 2013 blend is a question for the sommelier.

At thirteen years it is deep garnet. It is rich and polished: blackcurrant, black cherry, cocoa, cedar and violet, full in body with fine, firm tannin and a long finish.

It is on the list for the collector and the celebration. With the Chateaubriand, prime steak or lamb, its depth and polish make an occasion of the meal. A magnum of the 2015 is on the list for a bigger table.

value.a:
Caymus Special Selection 2018 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 16171, $480.

Caymus Vineyards is the Wagner family winery in Rutherford, in the Napa Valley, known for a ripe, plush style of Cabernet Sauvignon. Special Selection is its top wine. It is made only in some years, from the family’s best lots, and aged longer in oak than the Napa Valley Cabernet. The list prints it as Special Selection; you may also hear Special Select.

At eight years it is a deep, near-opaque ruby. It is opulent: black cherry, blackberry, cocoa, vanilla and sweet spice, very full in body, with velvety tannin and a long, rich finish.

It is on the list for the guest who loves Caymus and wants the grandest version, and for a celebration with the Chateaubriand for two or a prime steak. The Napa Valley Caymus is the sweet spot sibling.

value.a:
Dominus Estate 2014 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 17733, $495.

Dominus, DOM-ih-nus, is the Napa estate of Christian Moueix, of the Libourne family behind Pétrus and Trotanoy; our 1946 Trotanoy is the same family’s Pomerol. He farms the historic Napanook vineyard at Yountville, in the Napa Valley, and makes the wine with a Bordeaux sensibility: restraint, freshness and structure over sheer ripeness. It is Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot; the 2014 mix is a question for the sommelier.

At twelve years it is deep garnet. It is savory rather than sweet: blackcurrant, graphite, tobacco, dried herbs and earth, with firm, fine tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list for the Bordeaux lover who wants Napa, and for a quiet celebration over the Chateaubriand or lamb. An older Dominus, the 2001, is printed too.

value.a:
Heitz Cellar Martha’s Vineyard 2009 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 17761, $540.

Heitz Cellar was founded in St. Helena, in the Napa Valley, by Joe and Alice Heitz. Their Martha’s Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon comes from a vineyard in Oakville planted by Tom and Martha May, and it was one of the first Napa wines bottled under a vineyard’s name. It is famous for a signature note of mint and eucalyptus that guests who know it look for.

At seventeen years it is garnet with a brick rim. It tastes of blackcurrant, cedar, mint, eucalyptus and earth, the tannins softened, fresh and long.

It is on the list as Napa history in a glass: with many vintages printed back to 1997, it is a collector’s bottle and a celebration bottle. With lamb, herbs or the Chateaubriand, the mint and cedar sing.

value.a:
Opus One 2010 is a famous name in our celebration tier, sixteen years old: bin 145112, $775.

Opus One began as a partnership between Robert Mondavi, the Napa pioneer, and Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Château Mouton Rothschild in Bordeaux. The idea was one wine joining Napa fruit and Bordeaux craft, made at its own winery in Oakville, in the heart of the Napa Valley. It is a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with the other Bordeaux grapes, aged in new French oak.

At sixteen years it is deep garnet. It tastes of blackcurrant, black cherry, cedar, tobacco and cocoa, with silky tannin and a long finish; the age has made it seamless.

It is on the list because guests ask for it by name and dream of it with a great steak. With the Chateaubriand for two, prime steak or lamb, it makes the occasion. Several vintages and magnums are printed, so the sommelier can help a guest choose.
