value.a:
Harlan Estate 2006 is a famous name in our celebration tier, twenty years old: bin 16665, $1250.

Harlan Estate was founded by Bill Harlan on the western hills above Oakville, in the Napa Valley, with a clear ambition: to make a first growth of California. It is one of Napa’s cult wines, made in very small amounts and sold mostly to a mailing list. It is a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with the other Bordeaux grapes, aged in new French oak.

At twenty years it is deep garnet with a bricking rim. It tastes of blackcurrant, black cherry, cedar, graphite, tobacco and violet, dense yet silky, with a very long finish.

It is on the list for the collector and the once in a lifetime occasion. The list prints ten vintages from 2003 to 2015, a rare vertical, so the sommelier can guide a guest to the year that matters to them.

value.a:
Screaming Eagle Second Flight 2012 is a famous name on our list for a grand celebration: bin 181131, $1400.

Screaming Eagle is the most famous of Napa’s cult wines: a tiny estate in Oakville whose wine is sold almost entirely to a long-closed mailing list. Second Flight is its second wine, renamed The Flight, and it is rare in its own right. The 2012 is a Bordeaux blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc; the exact proportions are a question for the sommelier.

At fourteen years it is deep garnet. It tastes of cassis, plum, black olive, spice and earth, plush yet savory, with fine tannin and a long finish.

It is on the list for the collector who wants a Screaming Eagle experience, filed with the other red blends rather than the Cabernets. With the Chateaubriand at a grand occasion, it is a story as much as a wine.

value.a:
Ridge Three Valleys 2023 is the value bottle with the Creole Hanger Steak at dinner: bin 15142, $60.

Ridge Vineyards is one of California’s great Zinfandel houses, best known for Monte Bello in the Santa Cruz Mountains and Lytton Springs in Sonoma. Three Valleys is their Sonoma County blend, built on Zinfandel with Petite Sirah and other old field grapes drawn from several valleys there, and aged in oak. The exact 2023 mix is a question for the sommelier.

It is a young, deep purple. It tastes of blackberry, raspberry and black pepper with a little sweet spice, juicy and round, with soft tannin and bright acidity.

It is on the list as the friendliest way into Ridge, and it earns its place with spice. The chili crisp and Creole seasoning on the hanger steak make a firm, tannic red taste bitter; Zinfandel’s ripe fruit and soft tannin stay calm and juicy beside them.

value.a:
Piedrasassi Bien Nacido Vineyard Syrah 2021 is an anchor among our other reds under $100: bin 13362, $80.

Piedrasassi, pee-ay-drah-SAH-see, is the Syrah label of Sashi Moorman and Melissa Sorongon, made in Lompoc on the Central Coast of California. This wine comes from the Bien Nacido Vineyard in the Santa Maria Valley, a cool valley open to Pacific fog, where some of the oldest Syrah vines on the Central Coast grow. They make it in the style of the Northern Rhône in France, for savor and freshness rather than ripeness.

At five years it is a deep purple-ruby. It tastes of black cherry, black pepper, smoked meat, olive and herbs, medium in body, with fine tannin and lively acidity.

It is on the list for the guest who loves Rhône wine and the guest who wants something different from Cabernet. With grilled lamb, hanger steak or the burger, the pepper and smoke come alive.

value.a:
Ridge Lytton Springs 2022 is the sweet spot bottle with the Creole Hanger Steak at dinner: bin 16719, $120.

Lytton Springs is Ridge Vineyards’ estate in the Dry Creek Valley of Sonoma County. Its oldest vines were planted as a field blend, the old California way: Zinfandel growing side by side with Petite Sirah, Carignane and other grapes, picked and fermented together. Because Zinfandel is not always enough of the mix to name it on the label, Ridge calls the wine simply Lytton Springs. It is aged in American oak.

At four years it is a deep purple. It tastes of blackberry, black cherry, black pepper and clove, brambly and spiced, medium-full in body with firm but ripe tannin.

It is on the list as Ridge’s classic Zinfandel, and it is the sweet spot pairing for the dinner hanger steak: the spice meets the Creole seasoning, the ripe fruit loves the Madeira glaze on the broccolini, and it stands up to the chili crisp.

value.a:
Penfolds Bin 389 Cabernet Shiraz 2019 is an anchor among our other reds in the sweet spot: bin 121322, $145.

Penfolds is South Australia’s most famous wine house, the maker of Grange, and its wines carry bin numbers from the cellar. Bin 389 is its Cabernet Shiraz, a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz that Australia made its own. It is aged in American oak, including barrels that held Grange in an earlier year, which is why it is often called Baby Grange. The list prints Barossa Valley; the label usually says South Australia, which is a question for the sommelier.

At seven years it is a deep purple-red. It tastes of blackcurrant and plum with mocha, licorice and spice, full bodied with solid tannin.

It is on the list for the guest who loves big, rich reds and the Penfolds name, at a far gentler price than Grange, and for steak, lamb or the burger.

Kosta Browne was founded in Sebastopol, in Sonoma County, by Dan Kosta and Michael Browne, two restaurant workers who started making wine with tip money they had saved. It grew into one of California’s most sought-after Pinot Noir houses, which servers enjoy telling. This bottling is from cool vineyards on the Sonoma Coast, near the Pacific, made in a rich, polished style with French oak.

At five years it is a deep ruby. It tastes of black cherry, raspberry, cola and baking spice, ripe and silky, medium-full in body with smooth tannin.

It is on the list for the guest who loves Pinot Noir but wants more richness than Burgundy, and for duck, pork, salmon or mushrooms. A server’s story with a server’s favorite wine.

value.a:
Duckhorn Three Palms Vineyard Merlot 2020 is an anchor among our other reds in the sweet spot: bin 141234, $240.

Duckhorn Vineyards, the St. Helena winery founded by Dan and Margaret Duckhorn, made its name with Merlot, and Three Palms is the vineyard most tied to that story. It lies on a rocky alluvial fan on the valley floor near Calistoga, at the warm north end of the Napa Valley, and is named for three palm trees on the property. The stones drain well and keep the vines lean, which gives the wine concentration.

At six years it is a deep ruby-purple. It tastes of black cherry, plum, cocoa and cedar with a little herb, full and plush in body, with firm, velvety tannin.

It is on the list for the guest who loves Merlot and wants its grandest Napa expression, and for duck, roast pork, mushrooms or steak.

value.a:
Château Musar 2003 is an anchor among our other reds in the celebration tier: bin 33512, $285.

Château Musar was founded in Lebanon by Gaston Hochar and made world famous by his son Serge Hochar, who kept making wine through years of war. The grapes grow high in the Bekaa Valley, and the wine is made and aged north of Beirut. The red is a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cinsault and Carignan, aged in oak and then in bottle for years before release; its style is famously individual, with a wild, savory edge that collectors love.

At twenty-three years it is a garnet with an amber rim. It tastes of dried cherry, fig, spice, leather and incense, silky, with lively acidity.

It is on the list for the adventurous guest and the collector, and with five vintages printed it makes a story. With lamb, game or a cheese course, it is at home.

value.a:
Penfolds Grange 2004 is a famous name in our celebration tier, twenty-two years old: bin 11723, $650.

Grange is Australia’s most famous wine. Max Schubert, Penfolds’ chief winemaker, created it in the 1950s after a visit to Bordeaux, determined to make an Australian red that could age for decades. It is Shiraz, with a little Cabernet Sauvignon in most years, blended from old vineyards across South Australia and aged in new American oak. The list prints Barossa Valley; the label usually says South Australia, a question for the sommelier.

At twenty-two years it is a deep garnet. It tastes of blackberry, plum, mocha, licorice, leather and spice, dense and powerful, the ripe tannin softening into a long finish.

It is on the list for the collector and for the guest who wants the grandest Australian red, with the Chateaubriand, prime steak or lamb. Three younger vintages are printed too.

value.a:
Castello Banfi Florus 2011 is the value bottle with two desserts, the Blackberry Trifle and the Pineapple Tarte Tatin: bin 192345, $60.

Long before Brunello made Montalcino famous, the Tuscan hill town was known for a sweet wine called Moscadello, made from Moscato Bianco. Castello Banfi, the large estate founded there by the Mariani family, American wine importers, revived it with Florus: a late harvest wine from grapes left on the vine to ripen and concentrate, partly aged in oak.

At fifteen years it is golden amber. It tastes of honey, apricot, candied orange and orange blossom, with a little nuttiness from age and fresh acidity to keep it lively.

It is on the list as the gentlest priced dessert bottle, and it works twice. It is sweeter than the lemon curd and blackberry in the trifle, so it never tastes thin, and its honeyed, tropical fruit meets the charred pineapple and sweet anglaise of the tarte Tatin.

value.a:
Hexamer Meddersheimer Rheingrafenberg Riesling Spätlese 2010 is the value bottle with the World Famous Bananas Foster: bin 27501, $85.

Weingut Hexamer is a family estate at Meddersheim on the Nahe, a small Riesling region of Germany between the Mosel and the Rhine. Meddersheimer Rheingrafenberg names the village and the vineyard, its best known. Spätlese means late harvest: riper Riesling picked later, here made sweet.

At sixteen years it is a deep gold. The fruit has turned to honey, baked apple and apricot, with a little petrol and spice, the marks of aged Riesling, and the acidity is still bright and racy.

It is on the list because aged German Riesling is one of the great matches for caramel and fruit, at a friendly price. With the Bananas Foster, flambéed tableside in brown sugar, butter and rum, it is sweet enough to stand up to the caramel, and its acidity cuts through the butter so the dessert tastes lighter.

value.a:
Domaine des Baumard Clos Sainte Catherine 2006 is the value bottle with the Baked Apple on the breakfast tasting and with the New Orleans Bread Pudding: bin 19341, $90.

Domaine des Baumard, boh-MAR, is a family estate at Rochefort-sur-Loire, in Anjou in the Loire Valley. The Coteaux du Layon is the stretch of slopes along the Layon river where Chenin Blanc is left to ripen late for sweet wine. The Clos Sainte Catherine is Baumard’s walled vineyard there.

At twenty years it is a deep gold. It tastes of quince, baked apple, honey, apricot and a little ginger, sweet, with the lively acidity Chenin keeps for decades.

It is on the list because Chenin Blanc is the natural partner for apple, and this one has age at a friendly price. With the Baked Apple, its fruit echoes the apple and its sweetness matches the brown sugar glaze, while the acidity lifts the crème fraîche and the oat and pecan crumble. With the bread pudding, it is as sweet as the whiskey caramel, its honey meets the pralines, and its acidity keeps the custard from feeling heavy.

value.a:
Dr. Hermann’s Kranklei Goldkapsel Spätlese 2018 is the value bottle with two desserts, the Framboise French Toast and the Lemon Tart: bin 28461, $95.

Weingut Dr. Hermann is a family estate at Erden on the Mosel. This wine comes from the Kranklei, a parcel of the Ürziger Würzgarten, the spice garden of Ürzig, a steep vineyard of red slate above the river. Spätlese means late harvest, and the Goldkapsel, the gold capsule on the bottle, marks a richer selection within it. The list spells it Urziger Wurtzgarten; the label says Ürziger Würzgarten.

At eight years it is a pale gold. It tastes of white peach, apricot, lime, spice and slate, light in body and sweet, with electric acidity.

It is on the list because sweet Mosel Riesling is one of the few wines that survives lemon. With the Lemon Tart it stays bright against yuzu and meringue, and with the French toast it cuts the mascarpone and meets the raspberry coulis.

value.a:
Domaine Huet Le Mont Moelleux 2009 is the sweet spot bottle with the Baked Apple on the breakfast tasting: bin 33431, $135.

Domaine Huet, oo-ETT, is the great estate of Vouvray, in the Touraine of the Loire Valley, and is farmed biodynamically. It makes Chenin Blanc from three famous vineyards, and Le Mont is one of them. Each year Huet decides how sweet each vineyard’s wine will be: sec is dry, demi-sec gently sweet, and moelleux, mwah-LUH, properly sweet.

At seventeen years it is golden. It tastes of honeyed quince, baked apple, chamomile and beeswax, sweet and rich, with Chenin’s fresh acidity and a long, mineral finish.

It is on the list as one of the world’s great sweet Chenin Blanc wines with age on it. With the Baked Apple, it tastes like the apple itself; it is as sweet as the brown sugar glaze, and its acidity lifts the crème fraîche and the crumble.

Kracher Cuvée Auslese 2017 is the sweet spot bottle with the Pineapple Tarte Tatin: bin 19234, $190.

Kracher, KRAH-ker, is the most famous sweet wine house in Austria, at Illmitz on the eastern shore of the Neusiedlersee in Burgenland. The lake is wide and shallow, and its autumn mists help the grapes ripen and concentrate. Alois Kracher made the estate’s name around the world, and his son Gerhard runs it today. The Cuvée Auslese blends Welschriesling with Chardonnay, fermented and kept in steel to stay fresh; how much of each grape went into the 2017 is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is bright gold. It tastes of pear, quince, mandarin, passion fruit and orange blossom honey, creamy, sweet, with fresh acidity.

It is on the list for its tropical richness: with the Pineapple Tarte Tatin it echoes the charred pineapple and the sweet condensed milk anglaise.

value.a:
Château Climens 2010 is the sweet spot bottle with the Lemon Tart: bin 192821, $200.

Barsac is the village next to Sauternes in Bordeaux, on lower, limestone ground, and its sweet wines are known for a lifted freshness. Château Climens, klee-MAHNS, is a first growth of Barsac in the 1855 classification of sweet wines, farmed biodynamically. Unusually, it makes its wine from Sémillon alone. The grapes are picked by hand in several passes once noble rot has shrivelled and concentrated them, and the wine is aged in oak.

At sixteen years it is deep gold. It tastes of candied lemon, apricot, pineapple, honey and saffron, sweet and rich, but with a freshness that keeps it lively.

It is on the list as one of the great sweet wines of Bordeaux, and it suits the Lemon Tart because its citrus meets the yuzu and lemon jelly, and its honey loves the toasted meringue.

value.a:
Asked: What is noble rot?

Answer: A mold that shrivels ripe grapes in misty autumns, concentrating their sugar and flavor; it makes Sauternes and Barsac.

Asked: Is Barsac the same as Sauternes?

Answer: Barsac is a village inside the Sauternes area that may use either name; its wines tend to be a little fresher.

Asked: Why only Sémillon?

Answer: It is Climens’s way; most neighbors add Sauvignon Blanc.

value.a:
Inniskillin Cabernet Franc Icewine 2015 is the sweet spot bottle with the Blackberry Trifle: bin 192231, $225.

Icewine is made from grapes left on the vine into winter, picked while frozen and pressed while still frozen. The water stays behind as ice, and only a few drops of very sweet, concentrated juice come out. Inniskillin, in-ih-SKIL-in, founded by Donald Ziraldo and Karl Kaiser on the Niagara Peninsula of Ontario, made Canadian icewine famous around the world. Most icewine is white; this is a rare red, from Cabernet Franc. The list spells Peninsula with a double n.

It is pale ruby. It tastes of strawberry, raspberry, red cherry and rhubarb with candied fruit, intensely sweet with vivid acidity.

It is on the list as a conversation piece and a great match for berries. With the Blackberry Trifle, its red berry fruit echoes the blackberry curd, and its acidity stays fresh beside the lemon curd and coconut.

Its Amarone and Recioto, made from dried grapes, are among Italy’s most sought after wines. Recioto, reh-CHOH-toh, is the region’s old sweet red: Corvina, Corvinone, Rondinella and other local grapes are laid out to dry for months, pressed, and fermented until the wine is rich but still sweet.

At twenty-nine years it is a deep garnet. It tastes of dark cherry, blackberry, fig, raisin, chocolate and spice, sweet and velvety, with fresh acidity.

It is on the list as a true rarity, a sweet red from a legend. With the Blackberry Trifle, its dark berry fruit echoes the blackberry curd, and it is wonderful with chocolate or blue cheese.

Château Gilette Crème de Tête 1989 is the celebration bottle with the World Famous Bananas Foster: bin 19112, $515.

Château Gilette, zhee-LET, is a tiny estate at Preignac, in Sauternes, run by the Médeville family. It does something no other Sauternes estate does: it holds its wine for many years in small concrete vats, protected from air, and bottles and releases it only when it is ready, often two decades after the harvest. Crème de Tête, the cream of the top, is its best selection, Sémillon with a little Sauvignon Blanc. It was not ranked in 1855, and needs no ranking.

At thirty-seven years it is amber gold. It tastes of crème brûlée, caramel, dried apricot, orange peel and saffron, sweet, with a surprising freshness.

It is on the list as one of the great old Sauternes, and with the Bananas Foster, flambéed in butter, brown sugar and rum, its caramel depth is a match made at the table.

The pickers go through the vineyard many times, taking grapes one by one as noble rot concentrates them, and the wine is aged in new oak; in a poor year, no Yquem is made at all.

At nineteen years it is deep gold. It tastes of apricot, honey, candied orange, pineapple, vanilla and saffron, rich and sweet, with fresh acidity and an endless finish.

Barbadillo Pale Cream is our gentlest priced sweet wine and a first pick for the cheese board: bin 29801, $50.

Sherry comes from the southwest corner of Spain, around Jerez and the seaside town of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, where Bodegas Barbadillo, a family house best known for manzanilla, makes its wines. Most sherry starts dry, from the Palomino grape. A pale cream is a light, pale sherry made in the fino style and then gently sweetened, so it keeps a fresh, nutty edge.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of apricot, honey, almond and vanilla with a faint salty, nutty note, medium sweet and silky, with a soft, long finish.

It is on the list as the friendly sweet sherry: lovely chilled before dinner, and with the cheese board its salty, nutty edge meets the cheese. It is too lightly sweet for the bread pudding, which wants a sweeter wine.

value.a:
Feist Late Bottled Vintage Port 2006 is the value bottle with two desserts, the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and The Snickers: bin 193212, $60.

Port is the sweet fortified red of the Douro Valley in northern Portugal: grape spirit is added during fermentation, which stops it while the wine is still sweet. A Late Bottled Vintage, or LBV, comes from a single year and is aged several years in wood before bottling, so it is ready sooner than a vintage Port. Feist is an old Port house founded by two German cousins, today part of the Sogevinus group, known mostly for ruby and tawny Ports.

At twenty years this 2006 is unusually mature for an LBV. It tastes of black cherry, plum, raisin, cocoa and spice, sweet, with softened tannin.

It is on the list as the friendly Port for chocolate. Its cocoa and dark fruit meet the chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate of the coffee cake and the milk chocolate and caramel of The Snickers.

value.a:
Taylor Fladgate Quinta de Vargellas 1987 is the sweet spot bottle with the Cherries Jubilee: bin 19321, $185.

Taylor Fladgate is one of the great Port houses. Vintage Port is made only in the best years, when a house declares a vintage; it is bottled young and ages for decades in bottle. Quinta de Vargellas, in the Douro Superior, far up the river, is Taylor’s finest estate and the backbone of its vintage Ports. In good years that are not declared, Taylor bottles Vargellas on its own as a single quinta vintage Port, and 1987 was one of them.

At thirty-nine years it is a garnet with a tawny rim. It tastes of dried cherry, plum, violet, spice and fig, sweet, with softened tannin and a fine, long finish.

It is on the list as mature vintage Port at a sweet spot price. With the Cherries Jubilee, its cherry fruit and spice meet the flambéed black cherries, and its softened tannin sits gently beside the vanilla ice cream.

value.a:
Riveyrac Rivesaltes 1975 is the sweet spot bottle with the World Famous Bananas Foster: bin 193312, $190.

Rivesaltes, reev-SALT, is a vin doux naturel from Roussillon, in the far south of France near Perpignan and the Spanish border. Grenache and Grenache Gris are fermented, and grape spirit is added partway to stop the fermentation, leaving the wine sweet. The old wines are then aged for decades in old casks, where air slowly turns them amber and nutty. Riveyrac wines come from the cooperative cellar of Salses-le-Château, one of the oldest in the area.

At fifty-one years it is amber. It tastes of caramel, walnut, quince, marmalade, coffee and spice, sweet, with a delicate acidity that keeps it lively.

It is on the list as a half century of history at a sweet spot price. With the Bananas Foster, flambéed in butter, brown sugar and rum, its caramel and nut notes taste like the sauce itself.

Graham’s, GRAY-umz, is one of the great Port houses, owned by the Symington family, and its home estate is Quinta dos Malvedos in the Douro Valley of Portugal. Its vintage Ports are known for a rich, ripe, sweet style. Vintage Port is made only in years a house declares, bottled after about two years in wood and then aged in bottle, where it throws a crust; 2000 was a declared year.

At twenty-six years it is deep purple-garnet and still vigorous. It tastes of blackberry, black cherry, plum, chocolate, licorice and violet, sweet, with firm, ripe tannin.

It is on the list as vintage Port in its prime at a sweet spot price. With The Snickers, its grip and ripe fruit stand up to milk chocolate, caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts, where a lighter dessert wine would disappear.

value.a:
Dow’s 1985 Vintage Port is a first pick for the Cheese Board: bin 19221, $260.

Dow’s, DOWZ, is a Port house owned by the Symington family, with Quinta do Bomfim as its home estate in the Douro Valley of Portugal. Among the great houses, Dow’s is known for a drier style of vintage Port. Vintage Port is made only in declared years, bottled young and aged in bottle, where it throws a crust; 1985 was a declared year.

At forty-one years it is a garnet turning tawny at the rim. It tastes of dried plum, fig, raisin, cedar and spice with a little chocolate, sweet but mellow, the tannin softened into a long finish.

It is on the list as mature vintage Port for a celebration, and the cheese board is its natural partner. The sweetness balances salty cheese, and its drier edge stays fresh beside the seasonal chutney, Brennan’s honey and the fruit and nut bread.

Asked: What makes a vintage Port special?

Answer: It is made only in declared years, the finest, and ages for decades in bottle.

Asked: Is it still good at forty-nine?

value.a:
Henriques & Henriques Founder’s Solera 1894 is a famous name in our celebration tier and the oldest date on our list: bin 29088, $3200.

Madeira is the fortified wine of a Portuguese island in the Atlantic. It is aged warm, which gives it caramel and dried fruit and makes it nearly immortal; a bottle a century old can still be vivid, and an open one keeps for months. Henriques & Henriques is a historic Madeira house on the island. Its Founder’s Solera was begun in 1894: in a solera, wine is drawn from the casks and they are refreshed with other wine over the years, so 1894 marks the start, not a single harvest.

In the glass it is dark amber with a green rim. It tastes of dried fruit, toffee, dark chocolate, spice, honey and old wood, sweet, with piercing acidity and a finish that lasts minutes.

It is on the list as history in a glass, for the guest who wants to taste the nineteenth century.

classic.sayIt: For something special, Taylor Fladgate Quinta de Vargellas with age: mellow vintage Port, cherries and spice.

splurge.why: Bridge and sweet: a 1977 Taylor Fladgate vintage Port has dried cherry and spice that match the flambéed fruit.
splurge.sayIt: For a celebration, Taylor Fladgate 1977 vintage Port: almost fifty years old, silky and spiced, glorious with cherries.

value.sayIt: With the bread pudding, Baumard’s sweet Loire Chenin: honey, quince and baked apple, sweet enough for the caramel and bright to finish.
